news.title: CNN Data Shows MAGA Republicans Match Democrats in Midterm Voting Motivation
news.text:
MAGA Republicans are just as likely as Democrats to say they are certain to vote in the 2026 midterm elections, according to figures CNN presented Monday.

Among Democrats, 71 percent said they were certain to vote. The figure was also 71 percent among MAGA Republicans.

CNN’s Harry Enten also looked at whether President Donald Trump has lost support among MAGA Republicans since the 2024 election. Trump won 99 percent of the MAGA Republican vote against Kamala Harris, Enten said. His approval rating among the group now stands at 98 percent.

“Perhaps surprisingly, I might have thought it would be 100%, but it was 99%,” Enten said of Trump’s 2024 vote share.

Comparing that figure with Trump’s current approval rating, Enten said, “There’s been no real decline in MAGA support for the Trump administration.”

The figures show that Trump retains strong support among MAGA Republicans and that the same share of MAGA Republicans and Democrats say they are certain to vote in the midterms.

The report drew reactions online from people who said they were eager to vote and predicted Trump’s upcoming rallies would boost turnout.

news.title: Pennsylvania School District Forced to Rescind Policy to Hide Kids’ Gender Confusion from Parents
news.text:
Just to the west of Philadelphia sits largely middle-class and upper-middle-class Chester County, which still falls within the Philly metropolitan area. People aspire to live there, to buy houses there, and to raise their families there. It’s generally regarded as more affluent, safer, and offering a higher quality of life than living in the city of Philadelphia.

The county had once been reliably red politically, but now it’s considered a blue suburban area. Roughly 41% of the total registered voters in the county are Democrats; approximately 39% are Republicans. Independents make up the other roughly 20%.

It’s not so much the data on registrations as much as how the people, both Democrat and Republican, vote in the county. It’s solidly blue. In presidential elections, Kamala Harris won the county by over 14 points in 2024; Joe Biden carried the county by 17 points over President Donald Trump in 2020. In 2016, Hillary Clinton beat Trump in the county by 9 points.

So, in the spirit of you get what you vote for, parents in Chester County have been kept out of the loop by schools and their staffs on children’s “social transitions.” In other words, if your child is gender-confused and either considering transitioning, or in the midst of transitioning, Chester County Intermediate Unit 24 (CCIU) School District had policies in place to hide that information from you.

According to its website, the CCIU provides special education services to the 12 school districts in Chester County, which “includes services to nearly 86,000 school students and over 6,000 educators.”

More to the point, the district had maintained policy 103.2, which mandated that teachers hide in-school transitioning from students’ parents. It stated that, “Intermediate Unit personnel should not disclose information that may reveal a student’s transgender status or gender nonconforming presentation to others, including the student’s parents/guardians and/or other Intermediate Unit personnel, unless legally required to do so or unless the student has authorized such disclosure.”

Pretty clear, right? CCIU was not finished.

Transgender and gender nonconforming students have the right to discuss and express their gender identity and expression openly and to decide when, with whom, and how much to share such private information.When contacting the parent/guardian of a transgender or gender nonconforming student, Intermediate Unit personnel should use the student’s legal name and the pronoun corresponding to the student’s gender assigned at birth unless the student or parent/guardian has specified otherwise...When communicating with parents/guardians of transgender or gender nonconforming students, Intermediate Unit employees will refrain from the use of gender pronouns and refer to the student by name whenever practicable.The Intermediate Unit does not condone the intentional and/or persistent refusal to respect a student’s consistently asserted gender identity, or inappropriate release of information regarding a student’s transgender or gender nonconforming status. Such conduct shall be a violation of this Board policy, the policy stated.

It’s pretty clear that this policy not only prohibited staff from disclosing information on transitioning students, but also embedded in the policy itself was explicit coaching on exactly how to keep parents in the dark.

Usually policies detail the “what” of a situation, but not always the “how.” This policy went there and then some. The policy then very clearly instructed school district staff on implementation:

Based on the policy, the District requires that: a) Staff must affirm a student’s gender dysphoria by always utilizing a student’s preferred name and pronouns, based exclusively on a student’s, not their parents’ request;b) Staff cannot inform parents that their child has requested a different name and pronouns at school and must affirmatively hide that information if the parents are not already aware of that information; andc) Any District staff member who does not comply with the policy and practice will face disciplinary action.

Of course, the sorts of things that go unsaid any time a school district enacts a policy like this are how much latitude teachers and staff have on influencing children to question their own sexual identities. They’d prefer to pretend that sort of thing never happens and that these minors come up with the idea to transition all by themselves.

A U.S. Supreme Court ruling changed things

In a landmark SCOTUS case in 2026, Mirabelli v. Bonta, both parents and teachers challenged California state policies that required schools to keep information about students’ gender transitioning confidential from parents unless the students consented. These policies were very similar to the one at CCIU in Pennsylvania.

The parents sued over being excluded from any knowledge and decisions regarding their own kids’ gender confusion at school. These policies had been followed in California regardless of the parents’ religious values and beliefs, and the desire on the part of parents to be a part of their children’s mental healthcare.

But it wasn’t just the parents. Teachers joined the lawsuit because they did not want to be compelled to use the students’ new “preferred pronouns” and names at school, especially when they knew that the parents were in the dark and would have objected.

The primary holding of the Supreme Court was that the state of California cannot prevent schools from telling parents about their children’s efforts to engage in gender transitioning at school without the children's consent, or require that schools use children’s preferred names and pronouns regardless of their parents’ wishes. SCOTUS ruled that all of this is unconstitutional.

Two issues were at play. The court decided that the state’s policies were a First Amendment issue. The court ruled that the policies “likely trigger strict scrutiny” because they could interfere with a parents’ right to guide his or her children on their religious upbringing. These school policies were seen as an intrusion on this.

The other issue was one of “substantive due process” under the Fourteenth Amendment, which centers in this case on parental authority over their children’s upbringing. In other words, and this may be an over-simplification, but in a battle between who the children belong to – the state or the parents – the Constitution sides with the parents.

Some good news

In the wake of the SCOTUS decision, the Independence Law Center and the Alliance Defending Freedom sent a letter to the CCIU on behalf of an unidentified parent or set of parents of a child impacted by this policy. On May 11, Jeremy Samek, a lawyer for the Independence Law Center, sent a letter to CCIU explicitly calling for the district to rescind its policy 103.2 in light of the SCOTUS ruling.

We often joke about sending a “strongly worded letter” as an ineffectual tactic, but in this case, it was more than “strongly worded.” Samek’s letter used case law and the facts to paint the CCIU into a legal corner. He demanded not only that the policy be rescinded, but that the district actively communicate to all teachers that prior guidance on keeping gender identification confidential be disregarded.

And in a thinly veiled threat of possible litigation, he requested the district place a “litigation hold” on email records, documentation, social media accounts, and other data that reference the CCIU’s policy on gender issues.

That led to the CCIU’s decision at a board meeting on Sept. 16 to rescind that policy. PJ Media reached out to the Independence Law Center’s Randall Wenger, the Law Center’s chief counsel. He said that the SCOTUS decision in California paved the way for this district and others to change their policies.

“As a general matter, school districts want their policies to comply with the law,” Wenger said. “In light of the Supreme Court’s decision in Mirabelli v. Bonta and the (president’s) Executive Order on this issue, districts that encourage staff to conceal a child’s social transition from parents face significant legal risk.”

Of course, CCIU was not alone. According to the national nonprofit organization, Defending Education, across the country there are 1,219 school districts that still maintain similar policies. This covers 21,352 schools and a total of 12.3 million students. So, even with the SCOTUS ruling, some schools and school districts still need to be dragged kicking and screaming into constitutional compliance.

news.title: Former Obama aides claim Democratic donors are still holding back after being burned by 2024 loss
news.text: Former Obama advisers who host the "Pod Save America" podcast spoke Friday about the purported reasons some major Democratic donors are holding back money as the party sees encouraging signs ahead in November's midterm elections. At the Texas Tribune Festival last week, the podcast hosts shared their optimism over Texas turning blue because of Republican struggles in purple states. Dan Pfeiffer spoke about numerous factors working against Republicans, even in rural areas, but still warned that Democrats have far less money to work with, compared to the GOP. Tommy Vietor replied, "I think those spending restraints compared to the opportunity are why you're starting to hear some, you know, sort of operatives and candidates like voicing concern and frustration that some of the traditional like big, big donors of the Democratic Party, are not viewing this as the generational opportunity that it could be." THE SOROS POLITICAL MACHINE IS PUTTING MILLIONS TO WORK BEFORE ELECTION DAY — AND ZEROING IN ON KEY RACES "Because I was talking to someone today who was like, ‘Let me paint for you the like extreme optimistic picture,’ which is Democrats are not only winning on the generic ballot, but if you look at the top like most salient issues, we are crushing in those areas as well, which was not the case in 2024, right?," he continued. Vietor proposed that if the results of this midterm election resemble recent special elections where Democrats overperformed, "it is like truly a historic opportunity to win statewide races, congressional races, down-ballot, up and down. And it just feels like a moment when all the biggest donors in the party should be pushing all their chips in the table as aggressively as possible and not holding back for — I don't know what reason — Trump bothering them?" "Yeah, I think there has been a huge shift in the funding approach ... in the large donor community since 2024," Pfeiffer said. "Part of it is people still angry about how that election went and feeling like they lit a billion dollars on fire in that election, which is a fair quibble in some ways." "There are a lot of people who are very afraid of being targeted by Trump like that just that your business is going to be targeted," he continued. "You're going to have all of a sudden, you're going to the FBI is going to show up at your door. You're going to have regulatory scrutiny you wouldn't have before. And so that has limited money." CASH-STRAPPED DNC SHELLED OUT MORE THAN $800K TO NON-VOTING TERRITORIES LIKE VIRGIN ISLANDS WHILE IN DEBT Pfeiffer argued further that this midterm election could possibly lead to a scenario where "you're looking at one of the largest swings in American history, something where Democrats could pick up races we've never even thought possible," he said. "We've been using 2006 as like the most relevant example of an election because it's you know, it's an unpopular president, unpopular war, all of that. But it very well could be a little more like '94, where everything changes where it's a realigning election." Democratic consultant Julian Epstein rejected the podcasters' comments. "It's always funny to me how these group think 'insiders' parrot one another, even when they're 'consensus' is obviously wrong. The truth is that the so-called 'blue tsunami' is very likely overstated. The margin of error and the 40 battleground congressional districts is more like 2% right now, and we've consistently seen Republicans being undersampled in recent years," he told Fox News Digital. "Donors are holding back because the Democrats don't have any attractive, positive agenda," he continued. "Democrats have an even lower approval rating than the president. Democrats used to be about building; today they are about tax-and-spend redistributionist big government welfare. They are about the victim Olympics." "Try going out on the street and ask 10 voters to name three things Democrats stand [for] today. I doubt you'll find any that can," Epstein added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Republican consultant Mary Marslender suggested the podcasters may have a key point. "Yes, major Democratic donors are holding back, still frustrated by the fallout from the 2024 cycle and increasingly concerned about the party's direction," Marslender told Fox News Digital. "Kamala Harris’ failed presidential campaign spent a staggering $1.5 billion in just 15 weeks, losing the popular vote, the Electoral College, the Senate, the White female vote, and support among both Latino and working-class voters," she continued. "That’s the equivalent of spending $25,000 per hour only to lose nearly every key demographic and benchmark the campaign touted as strengths." "Major donors who contributed eight-figure sums in 2024 have noticed this poor return on investment and appear less willing to spend this cycle," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Additionally, many major Democratic donors have slowed or withheld contributions because of concerns about the Party’s shift toward socialist policies," Marslender added. "Unsurprisingly, calls to destroy the country’s financial institutions have not resonated well with wealthy Democratic supporters."

news.title: Anti-South Asian ‘hate speech’ has exploded online in US, report finds  - Jamaica Inquirer – Daily Jamaica
news.text:
Hate speech against Indians, Bangladeshis and Pakistanis in the United States has risen sharply online, according to a report that traces the surge to US President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and rhetoric, economic anxiety, and the South Asian community’s growing visibility in US life.

The report, titled “The Rising Tide of Anti-South Asian Hate in the United States”, by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH), published on Sunday, found that the monthly volume of hate towards South Asians in the US on the social media platform X rose 240 percent between January 2024 and June 2026, from 12,904 posts to 43,843.

Researchers identified more than 542,000 hateful posts on the platform between January 2025 and June 2026 alone towards people from South Asia living in the US, with five of the six highest-volume months falling at the end of that period.

The researchers used the United Nations definition of hate speech. They tracked recurring anti-South Asian slurs and narratives online, reviewing posts to exclude criticism that did not meet the UN threshold.

They found that nearly half of the hate posts on X accused South Asians of invading the US, stealing jobs or threatening the country demographically, while the derogatory slur “pajeet” and its variants showed up in 30 percent of hateful posts on X and 45 percent on fringe platforms.

Posts depicting South Asians as dirty or unhygienic grew by 171 percent on X, “the fastest of all narratives”.

The hate frequently collapsed South Asian ethnic and religious groups into one, with Indians, Pakistanis and Bangladeshis conflated with one another, and Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs and Christians also treated as a monolith.

So why now?

Racism against Indians, Bangladeshis and Pakistanis has a long history in the US, but researchers argue the current surge reflects a confluence of longstanding prejudices and new political and economic pressures.

The report points to the H-1B visa programme, which allows US employers to hire skilled foreign workers, as a major flashpoint. Indians account for more than 70 percent of H-1B visa holders, and researchers linked several spikes in anti-South Asian hate to political fights over the programme, such as when Trump imposed a $100,000 payment requirement on certain new H-1B petitions in September 2025.

“Such actions serve a powerful symbolic function, in the bargain reinforcing the hostility of Trump’s base toward South Asians,” said the report.

The report makes the same argument about the administration’s rhetoric, highlighting Trump’s speech at an AI summit in July 2025, in which he criticised US technology companies for outsourcing jobs to India, after which researchers saw a sharp spike in anti-South Asian rhetoric online.

As more recent examples, the report points to a since-deleted September 2026 Department of Homeland Security post titled “Transformers: Age of Deportations”, featuring a Sikh man identified as “Mr Singh” and telling him to “get off our roads”.

Days later, the Department of Education posted “Make College Football Great Again”, after Texas Republican Bo French had complained about the presence of South Asians at a University of Texas football game.

The report argues that such rhetoric reinforces the idea of South Asians as outsiders who “can never truly belong in the country”.

From ‘model minority’ to job thieves

Economic resentment is another factor, researchers wrote, with the success of some South Asians increasingly being weaponised against them.

Indian Americans once stereotyped as a “model minority” are now portrayed as “opportunists and cheats”, and South Asians are used more broadly as a scapegoat for anger over jobs and the economy.

This comes as South Asians have become increasingly visible in US politics, from former Vice President Kamala Harris and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani to Vice President JD Vance’s wife, Usha Vance, and politician Vivek Ramaswamy. The report documents racist attacks against figures across party lines and highlights how, for example, Mamdani’s primary and mayoral victories triggered spikes in anti-South Asian and Islamophobic abuse.

Researchers say both trends are now also tied up with “anxieties on the part of the majority about loss of status”, and feed the “Great Replacement Theory”, a conspiracy about the white population in Western countries being replaced by an orchestrated takeover.

Social media has also turned those narratives into targeted harassment.

Researchers found X accounts doxxing South Asians accused of taking jobs or committing visa fraud, while influencers have confronted people at their homes and workplaces and posted the encounters online. Doxxing refers to exposing a person’s private details, such as their home address, online.

In one example, right-wing influencer Sara Gonzalez posted a video to more than half a million followers in which the report says she harassed a South Asian person she accused of exploiting the H-1B programme.

Meanwhile, generative AI has made that content even easier to produce, researchers say, depicting South Asians as “filthy and unclean, sexually predatory, culturally backward, or a demographic threat”.

While the report tracks hate largely through what is happening online, researchers write that online hate “does not exist in isolation from offline forms of hostility”. It cites a July incident in which an Indian Muslim mall employee in Utah was repeatedly stabbed in an attack that federal prosecutors charged as a hate crime. In September, a Sikh truck driver was stabbed 17 times at a Wyoming truck stop.

“Online and offline hate can reinforce one another”, the researchers wrote, “as narratives, stereotypes, and forms of demonization move between digital platforms, political discourse, media, and everyday life”.

news.title: Kamala Harris' Former Campaign Chair Won't Commit to Backing Her in 2028
news.text: Mitch Landrieu, the former New Orleans mayor who co-chaired Kamala Harris' 2024 presidential campaign, says he is thinking about running for president himself. Asked whether he would support another Harris run, he declined to say yes. "I like her very much. I enjoyed serving with her. I thought she ran a good campaign under very difficult circumstances," Landrieu told Carlo Versano in an interview on Newsweek's The 1600 podcast. He stopped short of an endorsement though. "If she wants to run, everybody should run. I don't think we ought to be in the business of telling people what to do or what not to do," he said. "I think the country is looking for something different and something new." He closed his answer with advice for any 2028 hopeful. "If you feel like you got in your heart and your soul you feel you have something to give to the country, get out there and let the voters tell you whether or not you get to stay on the island." Responding to a question about whether he was mulling a presidential bid, Landrieu confirmed it. "I am thinking about it," he said. "I'll make a decision at the appropriate time." Watch: The 1600 The South as the Battleground Landrieu, a Democrat who also served as Louisiana's lieutenant governor and as President Joe Biden's infrastructure coordinator, said he cares more about what ordinary people can do than about who holds the White House. "Democracy is not self-operating," he said. "A president alone will not save us." He argued that neither the courts nor Congress can be counted on to check President Donald Trump. Republicans in Congress, in his view, are not restraining the president the way a Republican majority did with Richard Nixon. "The senators are not coming. The congressmen are not coming. The only people who can save this country are the people." Landrieu joined the show to talk about The Long Play, a docuseries he hosts for Crooked Media that travels through Southern states ahead of the midterms. The series rests on the idea that the South is where American politics is headed. He pointed to population movement as the driver. "People are moving out of California, or maybe not necessarily into Florida anymore but from Florida to North Carolina, or people are moving from New Jersey down to Tennessee," Landrieu said. "When people move, things change." Democrats, he said, have paid a price for writing off the region. "There has been a massive disinvestment politically in trying to build things in the South," Landrieu said. "If you want people to vote for you, you have to go see them, even if you've been losing." In Texas, he said, the Senate race between Democratic candidate James Talarico and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, could be closer than many expect. Landrieu attended a Talarico rally in Laredo and met people there who had voted for Trump three times and planned to back Talarico. "They said, we're very disappointed in the president. We voted for him three times. He said he was gonna do two things, stay out of wars and reduce our costs. He didn't do either one of those things," Landrieu said. The polls back him up. Siena College has Talarico ahead of Paxton 49 percent to 43 percent in a survey taken September 8 to 11, and Emerson College has it much tighter at 47 to 46. Emerson also found that Hispanic voters in Texas, who went for Trump in 2024, now lean Talarico by 15 points, 54 percent to 39 percent. On his home state, Landrieu was more cautious. Louisiana, he said, will be one of the last Southern states to shift toward Democrats, along with Mississippi. "My honest assessment is that it's a little bit harder than all the other states right now." A Warning on Litmus Tests Voters no longer sort themselves neatly by party, according to Landrieu. Working-class Americans feel the system is rigged against them, he said, and are losing patience with politicians who speak to them simply as Republicans or Democrats. Trump's numbers reflect that broader frustration, Landrieu warned. Most polling averages now put his approval at 33 percent and disapproval at 61 percent nationally, giving him a net rating of minus 28. In July, his net rating was minus 19. He also had a message for the far left of his own party. "If you're not with me a hundred percent, you're not with me at all. In my opinion, that is a losing proposition, politically, spiritually, economically and for our country," Landrieu said. As some Democrats have reconsidered or distanced themselves from positions associated with the progressive politics of the late 2010s, Landrieu has not backed away from one of his most controversial decisions as mayor. In 2017, he ordered the removal of four Confederate monuments in New Orleans, a move that drew fierce opposition at the time. Nearly a decade later, he said he has no regrets. “I'd do it twice as fast and I'd do more if I could,” he said, calling the monuments “a lie.” Landrieu also defended the Biden administration's infrastructure law against Democrats who say the White House was too slow to get projects built before the 2024 election. He said the administration pushed $800 billion out the door in under a year and a half and started 73,000 projects. He acknowledged the political payoff was limited. "Politically, it didn't help very much, I agree with that," Landrieu said. "But in terms of a good piece of public policy that's really gonna impact the future of the country, I stand by it." news.summary: Asked about backing Kamala Harris in 2028, Mitch Landrieu wouldn't commit and said he's thinking about running himself.

news.title: ABC13 looks at why there's been a lack of debates in statewide races on November ballot
news.text:
HOUSTON, Texas (KTRK) -- We are 36 days from Election Day, and something is missing from the top-of-the-ballot campaigns: none of them have debated one another.

It's not unheard of for candidates to decline debates. But it's rare in modern Texas politics to have no debates for the U.S. Senate, governor, and lieutenant governor, especially given that some of the current candidates have debated in the past.

James Talarico is running for the U.S. Senate against Ken Paxton. He's agreed to debate, but Paxton has not.

In fact, Paxton has never debated an opponent as a statewide candidate.

Gina Hinojosa has offered to debate Governor Greg Abbott. Abbott has not reciprocated. It's a first for Abbott-who debated Wendy Davis in 2014 during his first run for Governor, Lupe Valdez in 2018, and Beto O'Rourke four years ago.

Lt. Governor Dan Patrick has not said yes to a debate against Vikki Goodwin. He has not debated an opponent since 2014, when he faced off against then-Lt. Governor David Dewhurst in the primary and Leticia Van de Putte in the general election 12 years ago.

"It's unfortunate that we're not having them this year," Nancy Sims, a University of Houston political science lecturer and a veteran of political campaigns, told ABC13. "The largest percentage of voters consider themselves independent, and debates really are a tool candidates can use to persuade voters in their favor."

Ted Cruz is not on the ticket this year, but he debated opponents in all three of his races for the US Senate. In a close 2018 race, he debated Beto O'Rourke twice. And John Cornyn debated MJ Hegar six years ago.

"I honestly believe that a debate would empower their opponents further and that they're giving them free publicity if they deign to debate them," Sims said.

Do debates matter? Well, that's been up for debate for quite a while.

A Harvard study of 60 years of televised debates in different countries found they really did not affect Election Day. But Sims points to two years ago, and the debate between then-President Biden and President Trump. Biden's poor performance did make a difference.

"It caused him to drop out of the race. It caused Kamala Harris to come into the race. That debate became a defining moment for the 2024 presidential election," Sims said.

You can still see all of these candidates, Republicans and Democrats, in their television ads, online, or at in-person events across the state, but because the three Republicans at the top of the ballot have not agreed to debate, you may not get to see them live and unfiltered on the same stage with their Democratic opponents.

"You get to hear from the candidates in a way that is different from their owned and paid for messages," Sims said. "The voter loses. Democracy includes things like debates, so the voter is who loses out."

ABC13 did reach out to the campaigns for Paxton, Abbott, and Patrick. As of late Monday, none of them had responded to our request for comment about the lack of debates.

"The largest percentage of voters consider themselves independent, and debates really are a tool candidates can use to persuade voters in their favor," Sims said. "I honestly believe that a debate would empower their opponents further and that they're giving them free publicity if they deign to debate them."

news.title: Trump Was Asked What He Really Thinks About Women In Leadership — And He Just Said The Quiet Part Out Loud
news.text:
President Donald Trump did not mince words when asked about the notion of women in charge of governments and former President Barack Obama’s suggestion that the world would improve under female leadership.

During an event with historian Doris Kearns Goodwin at Salem State University last week, Obama remarked that during his time in office, he “sometimes fantasized about, if you put women in charge of every government for like two years, and then just kind of saw, all right, how are things going?”

“I have a strong belief that things would ― they wouldn’t be perfect ― but they’d be better. I’m confident about that,” he added. 

While speaking to the press on Saturday, Trump responded to a question about the 44th president’s claim.

“Barack Obama just said if you put women in charge of every government for two years, things would be better. Do you buy that?” one reporter asked. 

“It’s a ridiculous ― I love women, I think they’re great, but what a ridiculous statement that is, right? Even you would say that,” Trump replied. 

Experts in politics and gender studies say the president’s remarks in the interview are quite telling. When asked about the president’s remarks, the White House referred HuffPost to Trump’s original comment.

“Obama is empirically right that the world would look radically different if women were in charge,” Caroline Heldman, a professor of political science and the chair of gender, women and sexuality studies at Occidental College, told HuffPost. “Decades of research finds that women world leaders have different policy priorities, governing styles, ethics, foreign policy approaches and responses to crises than men leaders.”

She noted that women officeholders tend to give more attention to issues like healthcare, education, childcare, parental leave, pay equity and violence against women.

“They place greater emphasis on collaboration, consensus-building and cross-party coalitions; demonstrate lower levels of corruption; are more likely to favor diplomacy, multilateral cooperation and humanitarian aid; and are more effective in reaching peace agreements,” Heldman added. “During COVID-19, women-led countries acted earlier, followed expert guidance more closely, communicated more clearly and saw better health outcomes.”

She was careful to note that none of this is about biology or innate differences ― but rather stems from “gendered socialization, the expectations placed on women leaders and the pressure women face to prove their competence in male-dominated institutions.”

Heldman also presented a thought experiment to get a sense of how different the world could be if women were in charge. 

“Imagine how different the U.S. would look if half of our presidents from the start had been women,” she said. “How would the U.S. be different if Hillary Clinton were elected in 2016? I assure you that had Kamala Harris been elected in 2024, we would not be in a foreign quagmire in Iran, we would not be paying $6.36 in California for gas, we would not be paying an average of $1,700 in extra household costs from new tariffs and we would actually know what’s in the Epstein files.”

Political scientist Shauna Shames, an associate professor at Rutgers University-Camden who studies gender and American politics, offered two reads of Trump’s remarks.

“The less charitable read ... is that Trump may indeed love women, but for certain things only, and not when they wield political power,” she said. “When they do, he tends to give them pretty awful nicknames and do a lot of mocking and ridicule. It is the first refuge of an insecure man.”

Throughout his time in the spotlight, Trump has lobbed several insults at women, from calling leaders like Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris “nasty” to going after celebrities like Jessica Chastain (“not hot”), Bette Midler (“extremely unattractive”), Stormy Daniels (“horseface”) and Rosie O’Donnell (“fat” and “a pig”).

And then there are all of his attacks on female reporters ― including telling Bloomberg’s Catherine Lucey “Quiet, piggy!”, dismissing CNN’s Kaitlan Collins as “very dumb and unhappy,” dubbing Maggie Haberman “Maggot Hagerman” and calling The New York Times’ Katie Rogers “ugly.” 

“Donald Trump’s claim that he loves women is not borne out by his dismissal of their superior leadership, nor the reports of serious sexual abuse against him,” Heldman emphasized. 

Kari Winter, a professor of global gender and sexuality studies at the University of Buffalo placed Trump’s dismissal in a broader context.

“According to the International Committee of the Red Cross, military conflicts are escalating globally to the tune of approximately 130 armed conflicts across 60 countries,” she said. “Donald Trump’s administration responds by calling for testosterone shots and greater lethality. After launching a reckless war of choice against Iran, Trump in his United Nations speech brought enormous shame on the United States by threatening the ‘annihilation’ of an ancient civilization.”

Winter was equally pointed about Trump’s track record more broadly.

“Listening to the doomsday scenarios that Trump and his bombastic ilk casually, stupidly and unimaginatively spout day after day, the world can observe that Trump excels at generating horrific new problems,” she said. “At the same time, it appears that he has never met a problem that he was capable of solving.”

As for Trump’s specific response to Obama’s comments, there was a clear familiar pattern.

“Given the dire state of the male-dominated world, Barack Obama’s invitation for us to imagine a world led by women makes a lot of sense. But Trump cannot imagine a better world,” Winter said. “In his nine-second response to the reporter’s question, he hits three of his habitual knee-jerk notes: disrespecting women, demeaning reporters, and dismissing as ‘ridiculous’ any idea to which he cannot formulate a reasoned response. His statement reveals nothing new. It hits the same sour notes we’ve heard time and again, ad nauseam.”

Shames also offered what she called an “extremely charitable read” of Trump’s “unbelievably sexist and idiotic remark” about women in government by examining the role of privilege in shaping his worldview. 

“Trump’s response to the reporter’s question surprises me not at all,” she explained. “One of the nicest things about having privilege ― and Trump has generally had just about every kind you can think of ― is that you don’t see it. So you don’t generally think about people who don’t get it. So the widespread and systematic exclusion of women from political power, not just here but generally worldwide, is probably never something that has entered Trump’s pampered, highly protected mind.”

She questioned whether Trump has any grasp of (or interest in) the historical barriers women have faced in political life.

“If I spouted the statistics about how little political power women have compared to their proportion of the population, he would call it fake news, I am sure,” Shames said. “And since he seems to have no understanding of history, the idea that the government itself has played no small role in preventing women from not only running for office, but doing things like serving on juries and even voting for the majority of American history would not get through to him.”

I'm not going to be one of those guys who scream that the polls are fake and we’re actually winning big, but I've been doing this long enough to recognize the signs that public polling is off and to notice when even the candidate knows it.

Iowa was never competitive. Ann Selzer, despite her reputation, was just wrong, wrong, wrong.

Michigan's U.S. Senate race is a different story.

It's definitely competitive, even though it probably shouldn't be. Democrats nominated socialist Abdul El-Sayed, and while most polls show him with a slight lead, he just handed us a huge sign that his campaign thinks he's behind.

El-Sayed built his political brand on Medicare for All. For years, he pushed a plan that would ban private insurance and force every American onto a single government plan. That same year, he acknowledged that Medicare for All "eliminates your private" health care plan. He kept at it in 2020. "What Medicare for All does is it does away with the private insurance market. Around the same time, he declared that "Medicare for All comes in and says 'no more of this insurance industry,'" and described private insurance as a "middleman" that should be "cut out."

"We are going to create one insurer," El-Sayed promised in 2021. He also claimed his plan would eliminate private health insurance and create "one insurance program for everyone," while insisting the health insurance industry "does not need to exist" and "should not exist."

news.title: Susan Collins Faces New Headwind as Maine Heating Costs Hit Record High
news.text: Senator Susan Collins is facing a new economic headwind in her reelection bid as home heating oil prices surge to a record high ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Rising fuel prices have emerged as a key vulnerability for Republicans nationwide as they defend their majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate, with only about 5 weeks until the midterms. Rising costs are attributed to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, a key passageway for global oil, amid the Iran war. Collins faces a unique challenge in Maine, the state most reliant on home heating oil. More than 50 percent of Maine residents use oil as their primary heat source, according to the Northeast Gas Association, and prices have steadily increased as winter approaches, adding pressure to Mainers’ finances as they weigh whether to elect Collins to another term. Home heating prices averaged $6.02 per gallon statewide last week, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources (DOER). That marks an increase from $3.33 per gallon one year earlier, and more conservative, rural parts of the state are facing especially high costs. The previous high was recorded in May 2022, when prices hit $5.92 per gallon as the nation grappled with a post-pandemic inflation wave. Heating costs are “always front of mind in Maine,” even in the “middle of the summer,” Mark Brewer, a professor of political science at the University of Maine in Orono, told Newsweek. “It’s cold here. Winter is long. It’s definitely a huge concern, even in years where fuel costs aren’t high. When they reach the point where they are right now, and they’re projected to go even higher, it’s definitely going to be a big issue,” he said. “No doubt about it.” Newsweek reached out to the Collins and Jackson campaigns for comment via email. Collins’ Reelection Bid Complicated by Rising Home Heating Prices Rising home heating prices threaten to complicate Collins’ reelection. She already faces a toss-up race against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate president, and affordability remains a central concern for voters both in Maine and across the country. The Iran war has not been popular in the polls. Trump’s approval rating has fallen after launching strikes against Tehran in February, as voters blame him for rising costs caused by the war. If voters blame Trump for rising home heating prices, Collins “is going to get some of that” heat, Brewer said. “She’s not Trump, obviously, but Trump is the president of her party, and Troy Jackson and his supporters are already making the argument that Collins is a Trump enabler, so this could definitely come back and bite her,” he said. Costs in Northern and Central Maine, which are the state’s more conservative regions, are even higher, averaging $6.05 and $6.09 per gallon, respectively. Jackson is not going to win those regions, but he could chip away at Collins’ margins there by focusing on heating prices, Brewer said. “If Troy Jackson can whittle away there, and he can do it using high heating costs as a chisel, that’s certainly going to help him,” he said. Meanwhile, Collins is likely to highlight her efforts to ensure federal support for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), which provides funding for low-income households’ energy costs in Maine, he said. Democrats Criticize Collins Over Heating Prices Jackson has criticized Collins over rising heating prices. “The best time to stop a war is before it starts. Susan Collins repeatedly voted to let Trump’s disastrous war in Iran continue. Now Mainers are paying through the nose for gas, diesel, and heating oil. What the hell is she good for?” he wrote in a September 17 post on X. Maine Democratic Party spokesperson Misha Linnehan also released a statement on Monday criticizing Collins’ position on the war. Collins initially voted against War Powers Resolutions that would have restricted Trump’s ability to wage war but started voting in support of those resolutions in April, citing its “clear 60-day deadline for Congress to either authorize or end U.S. involvement in foreign hostilities.” Linnehan wrote that the risks were “clear” the moment Trump began the “reckless war.” “Now, as the weather gets colder, Maine families are paying more than ever before to heat their homes, and there’s no end to the war in sight,” Linnehan wrote. Collins Presses Trump on Oil Prices Collins and Senator Angus King, a Maine independent, sent a letter to Trump last week urging him to release supply from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to lower costs for Mainers. “Maine is particularly vulnerable to global supply shocks because our state imports much of our home heating oil. With both domestic and international supplies running low, a release from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve would help ease these prices,” the letter reads. In April, Collins announced that $421 million in LIHEAP funding was released for the program, which she said provides “vital relief to thousands of Mainers” that helps them “avoid the constant worry of choosing between heating their homes and covering other basic necessities.” Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson: What Latest Polls Show About Maine Senate Race Polls have shown a close race between Collins and Jackson. A recent poll from The New York Times, The Portland Press Herald and Siena University released on Thursday showed Collins up 3 points, 49 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 619 likely voters from September 15 to 22. But other polls released last week showed Jackson leading Collins. Jackson led by 4 points in a University of New Hampshire poll, with 51 percent support to Collins’ 47 percent, up from July, when he led by 3 points. It surveyed 1,312 likely voters from September 17 to 21 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. Another poll from the University of Massachusetts Lowell gave Jackson a 5-point lead, 48 percent to 43 percent. Among independent voters, a critical voting bloc in the Pine Tree State, he led by 8 points, 40 percent to 32 percent, with 22 percent still undecided, the poll found. Collins and Jackson were tied in an InsiderAdvantage poll, which showed them both at around 46 percent. It surveyed 1,200 likely voters from September 22 to 23, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. Can Susan Collins Defy a Blue Wave? Notably, the 2020 race between Collins and Democrat Sara Gideon saw a polling error in Collins’ favor, though polling errors don't always repeat from cycle to cycle. Collins trailed Gideon in nearly every poll but ultimately outperformed the polls to hold onto the seat, even as former President Joe Biden won the state by 9 points that year. Democrats note that 2026 is likely to be a stronger national environment. Still, Maine is a difficult state to poll due to its older, rural population. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won Maine by about 7 points in 2024, but Collins has won in the past because of her personal popularity and bipartisan image. Democrats believe that a strong national environment this year could give them their best chance yet at unseating the longtime incumbent. Still, Republicans view the race as competitive and have hoped to cast Jackson as too progressive for the state. Democrats have also had a tumultuous election season in the state. Graham Platner, a progressive political newcomer whose campaign garnered national attention, was hit with sexual abuse allegations just weeks after clinching the nomination. He has denied the allegations but ultimately withdrew from the race. Jackson, who initially ran for governor but lost the primary, emerged as the new nominee during a convention in July, easily securing the required delegates to find his place on the ballot. What Do Prediction Markets Show? Prediction markets favor Jackson to flip Maine. As of Monday, he had a 61 percent chance on both Kalshi and Polymarket of winning against Collins. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. Why the Maine Senate Race Matters in 2026 Midterms Democrats’ path to a Senate majority runs through Maine. Democrats are increasingly hopeful about winning the Senate despite a difficult map. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, so Democrats must flip four seats to win control if they win every race in a seat they currently hold. Vance serves as the tiebreaker in a split Senate. To flip the Senate majority, Democrats must win every seat they currently hold, flip GOP-held seats in competitive states, and win some seats in more traditionally conservative territory. Democrats are defending seats in Trump-won states Georgia and Michigan. In addition to Maine, they view a GOP-held seat in North Carolina as a top flip opportunity. The race in New Hampshire, which backed Harris by about 3 points, is also competitive. No other Senate races are in Harris-won or single-digit Trump states, meaning Democrats must expand the Senate battleground and compete in more conservative areas if they want to win the majority. They are targeting GOP-held seats in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas as potential states to flip. The Cook Political Report classifies those four races as tossups. What Happens Next The Maine Senate race is expected to remain one of the most competitive battlegrounds of this year’s midterms, with forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball classifying it as a pure toss-up. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: Mainers are facing surging home heating prices as winter approaches, creating a new challenge for Collins' reelection bid.

news.title: 15 planes violated a temporary flight restriction over Chicago area during Trump's visit to Medinah Sunday
news.text:
Fifteen civilian planes violated a temporary flight restriction that was in place on Sunday during President Trump’s nine-hour trip to Illinois, with flares being deployed at two planes who did not initially respond to F-16 military jets flying alongside their wings.

Trump landed at O’Hare Airport at 9:40 a.m. to attend the Presidents Cup golf tournament in suburban Medinah. Air Force One was wheeled up at O’Hare at 6:40 p.m. During that time, the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) put in place a VIP temporary flight restriction over the Chicago area. 

NORAD says 15 general aviation aircraft violated the temporary flight restriction. NORAD fighter aircraft, including F-16s, were deployed as a “standard precautionary measure to ensure airspace security and establish visual contact with the unresponsive aircraft,” NORAD said in a statement.

In 10 of those instances, fighter aircraft performed tactical intercepts to get the attention of the pilots. During two of those intercepts, flares were dispensed which may have been visible to the public. Those flares were used to ensure pilots saw the NORAD aircraft and to communicate with the pilots, the agency said.

“All 15 situations were safely resolved with the aircraft escorted out of the restricted airspace,” NORAD said. 

During flight restrictions, pilots are expected to pay attention to NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions), which are filed with aviation authorities to notify pilots about airspace restrictions and hazards. During an interception, two fighters approach the plane, with pilots usually only seeing one, according to NORAD. The intent is to identify the plane and try to figure out why it’s in restricted space and encourage them to communicate with air traffic controllers. The fighter jets can also help escort the plane out of the airspace. If that doesn’t work, flares are deployed to get the attention of the pilot. 

The Federal Aviation Administration on Monday said it investigates all flight restriction violations and takes “appropriate action.” The agency said it does not discuss open investigations and referred questions to the U.S. Northern Command and the U.S. Secret Service. The agency said sanctions range from warnings to license suspensions or revocations, based on the circumstances of the violation.

Sunday marked Trump’s first visit to Illinois during his second presidency. He last came to Chicago in July 2024 during a combative interview at the National Association of Black Journalists conference, where he questioned the racial identity of Vice President Kamala Harris and lambasted a moderator’s question about derogatory statements he has made toward the Black community.

news.title: California AG Refuses to Admit His State’s Climate Agenda Has an Affordability Problem
news.text:
Cost of living is the name of the game in politics right now. Prices remain too high, household budgets are stretched thin, and voters are demanding a long-overdue reset. Yet California politicians appear to be operating in a different universe, one where the state’s high costs are not a warning sign, but a point of pride. 

In an interview with POLITICO released Monday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta was asked whether the state’s heavy-handed environmental regulations conflict with voters’ desire for lower costs. Rather than acknowledge the obvious tension, Bonta delivered a word salad worthy of Kamala Harris. He boasted about California’s role as the world’s fourth-largest economy, its so-called protections for workers and consumers, and its environmental initiatives. Bonta’s argument, in effect, was that California is not out of touch, it is simply “leading.”

"Aren't you a little bit worried that your climate pursuits seem a little out of touch with everyday Americans?"

"California is going to be California," Bonta said. "And that means leading, that means pushing, that means being on the front foot, that means leading with facts and science. And California has always been a leader. We've led with being the fourth largest economy in the world. We've led with protections for workers and consumers. We've led with our environmental initiatives. We will continue to lead. And oftentimes, we go first and others follow."

"So leading to do something that's important to do and the right thing to do doesn't mean out of touch. It means you're leading. And it means you're inspiring and you're showing the way and you're shining light on a path that we need to go down together," he added. "So no, I don't think we're out of touch. I think we lead. And I think that the next governor of California will have his ability to put his mark on California. I don't expect him to be the same as Governor Newsom. He will be Xavier Becerra. And I look forward to partnering with him and advancing California's including protecting our natural resources and advancing our environmental goals."

In other words, so long as California can claim it is “leading,” whether in environmental mandates, regulatory ambition, or simply the cost of staying afloat, Bonta and the state’s Democrat establishment seem perfectly willing to make the tradeoff on the public’s behalf. Rising utility bills, housing costs, fuel prices, and grocery tabs are apparently just the admission fee for being governed by people who confuse expensive with successful policy.

California may indeed lead the nation in plenty of categories, but it is only a matter of time before the state’s Democratic supermajority squanders the very successes it so consistently cites as proof of its good leadership.

news.title: I spoke to Joe Biden moments after THAT embarrassing meltdown against Trump... I abandoned the party and became a Republican after witnessing the shameless deception of Americans
news.text:
It was the night of June 27, 2024, and Lindy Li could feel her whole body shaking. She wasn't sure if it was intense hunger after a stressful day with no food, or the shock of seeing one of her heroes crumble in front of the entire nation.

The 81-year-old President, Joe Biden, had just put in a devastatingly shambolic debate performance against Donald Trump – the moment his attempt at a second presidential term tanked. Li, a prolific Democratic Party fundraiser, claims to have been one of the first people with whom he spoke on his arrival at the location where party loyalists had been watching the president's dismal showing on big screen TVs.

'I was shaking... like, I cannot believe this happened. I knew he was slowing down, that's no secret, but I didn't know he was going to face plant,' Li told the Daily Mail. 'I didn't know it was going to be an outright collapse. It was just embarrassing [and] painful to watch.'

As an avowed Democratic Party insider, Li, 35, had a front row seat to the implosion of Biden's campaign for re-election and the subsequent ascension of his Vice President Kamala Harris to the ticket, only for her to suffer a crushing defeat to Donald Trump.

Speaking to the President afterwards, she felt sorrow at the diminished figure before her. 'I had so much compassion for him, I didn't mention the debate -- I consoled him,' she told the Daily Mail. '[I felt] love and pity – actual pity – and that is not the feeling you want to have for your President.'

Now, when Li thinks back on what she recalls as an excruciating time, her overwhelming feeling is not compassion and sadness, but anger and guilt about all her friends and contacts who opened their wallets and gave her millions of dollars for what she claims the Democrats always knew was a losing cause.

As she exposes in her new book - Unburdened: A Former Democratic Insider's Shocking Account of Political Power, Betrayal, and Party Collapse, out on Tuesday – the former Liberal fundraiser not only lost faith in her party but switched sides entirely. So disenchanted was she by the millions she claims she saw squandered in behind-the-scenes excesses, the 'cult'-like mentality she alleges was fostered and the Biden family's and closest advisors' seeming desperation to cling to power.

She writes that Biden was 'shamelessness in human form,' while Harris is dismissed as the 'Cackle Queen.'

But perhaps what bites the most is the extent to which she feels she played a part in the deception she said she witnessed behind closed doors: '[People] were donating to the campaign because of their faith in me, and that propelled my need for accountability afterwards, because I felt like it was a personal betrayal.'

Today, Li doesn't hold back on the blame. Some of the most shocking claims in her book relate to what she alleges Democrats – and specifically Harris – spent in donor money on fripperies such as the Vice President's hairstyle, celebrity endorsers and frivolous gift baskets.

Breaking the code of loyalty and openly criticizing the Democratic Party in the aftermath of the November 2024 election defeat, Li switched her allegiance to the Republican Party in December 2024.

Li has earned herself plenty of enemies for such a polarizing move, but she feels like her life has toughened her to the blows she has faced in the past year.

Li was born in China, but when she was two weeks old her parents left her with her grandmother to move to Sheffield, England. She joined them when she was three years old in 1994, spending two years in the UK before relocating again to the United States.

After moving around for her father's job in academia, they settled in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania when Li was nine. Her father transitioned into real estate, making good money and catapulting the family into the upper echelons of Philadelphia society.

'I went to college with billionaires,' she said. 'That's just my life.'

Despite parents who Li said 'very much wanted me to be a traditional East Asian wife,' she was instead drawn to politics. She studied philosophy at Princeton where she was class President for each of her four years at the university.

After graduation, she joined Morgan Stanley as a wealth manager but quit in 2015 at age 25 to run for Congress in Pennsylvania's Democratic primary.

Even though she describes herself as socially conservative, she was swept up in the optimism of the first Obama administration, and it was an automatic assumption among her liberal peers at college that she would join the Democrats.

'I was told the other side consisted of Nazis, so it didn't even compute,' she said.

Her first attempt to run for office in 2016 failed when the signatures for her Pennsylvania candidacy were deemed invalid. Her opponent in the race had challenged her nominating petition, alleging she did not receive the required 1,000 signatures due to invalid signatures – the notary, Li said, had stamped but not signed them. She withdrew from the race.

'I take full responsibility,' she said at the time. 'I understand it is my job to make sure that it's done correctly.

'I've learned my lesson and no one will be able to exploit my weaknesses in the future.' 

And so, in 2018, she tried again. She came sixth in that primary, but she had caught the eye of the Democratic Party for other reasons: She had raised a large sum of money for a 27-year-old candidate with little political experience. Li claimed in media interviews that she raised $600,000 but the Federal Election Committee shows she received just over $168,000.

And so began Li's ascent to the top tiers of Democratic fundraising. Working the phones, schmoozing her contacts in society and businesses and hosting extravagant soirees attended by top Democratic figures on the rooftop pool of her luxury apartment, Li threw herself into the task of getting Biden elected for a second term.

'I wanted to lift him up, I loved him so much,' she said.

That deep loyalty meant that she was among the many insiders who, she claims, initially put on their blinders as Biden's frailty became clear during the second half of his Presidency.

But even as she appeared on TV and social media gushing about the president's competence, she admitted, she was engulfed with a creeping sense that he was ill equipped to lead the nation for a second term.

She also bristled at her own treatment in the party claiming she was pigeonholed into Asian American lobbying groups that she felt little identification with. 'The DNC imprisoned me in a racial silo against my will,' she writes in Unburdened, recalling a Democratic National Convention event at which she was asked to attend alongside a dancing Chinese lion.

Li maintains in her tome that those close to Biden – including his wife Jill and his son Hunter – knew that he did not have the capacity to serve another term but were seduced by their proximity to power and did everything they could to hide his age-related decline.

Both Jill and Hunter have point blank rejected the suggestion they had any sense that Biden was unfit for office, though Jill said in her own memoir that, on seeing her husband's disastrous debate performance she wondered whether he was 'having a stroke,' writing that she had, 'never ever seen Joe like that before or since.'

'The campaign had long since narrowed to a single, obsessive priority: Shielding the fragile ego of one aging leader rather than safeguarding the republic he swore to serve,' Li writes.

While Li also confessed to keeping up the charade immediately after the debate, she appeared on Fox News on July 21, one month after the debate aftermath, saying it was 'not my place to tell President Biden what to do but if he were to step aside, Vice President Kamala Harris would be an excellent candidate.'

Her timing was fortuitous: Later that same day, Biden announced that he was stepping down. Then came what Li sees as the second betrayal: the anointment of Harris to the Presidential ticket without any primary voting process.

Despite an initial swell of optimism, Li claimed that Democratic Party insiders knew Harris was a flawed candidate but rushed to anoint her anyway, given the lack of time until the election and the potential negative optics of overlooking a Black woman for the position. For her part, Li said, it took her only a week to raise $2 million for Harris, whereas it was a full year to bring in $1.1 million for Biden.

Still, she accused the party of 'enthroning a deeply inadequate woman as the spearhead in their battle against Trump and exchanging a cognitively broken man for a cognitive mediocrity.'

Li claimed she was pressured into publicly praising Harris on television and on her social media accounts, as well as keeping the donor money flowing, only to see it squandered on concerts with celebrities, endless goody bags for donors and even, she claimed, $69,000 in styling. In fact, the Daily Mail obtained Harris's campaign filings, which showed she spent $1 billion in her losing bid, including paying $69,000 to crew who worked on a Vogue magazine feature.

'I would get care packages every three weeks, and I knew I was raising the money for it, which is the oddest thing,' Li told the Daily Mail. 'That's my money that they're just blowing on trinkets. Why are you preaching to the converted?'

The Daily Mail has reached out to representatives for Harris for comment.

In the months that followed, Li claimed there were conflicts of interest among top staff and a revolving door of White House staffers into consulting firms that receive the donor money. All the while, she attended a host of DNC events that she described as 'a game of whack-a-celebrity, a bacchanal of self-congratulation and coastal elitism, the smell of uncut money wafting in the air.'

So, when the results came in on November 5, Li said she was devastated but not surprised. Soon after, she started appearing on the TV networks, discussing the flaws in the Harris campaign.

Her friends in the Democratic Party, she claims, swiftly turned on her. Cast into the political wilderness, she finally found acceptance among the conservative pundits and podcasters.

Today, she describes herself as a 'conservative-leaning independent.' While critics allege she is an opportunist happy to do a complete ideological U-turn to be close to power, she insists she is motivated by a desire to fix the country.

Li does not define herself as a member of the MAGA movement despite fundraising Trump's inauguration. She does not support the Iran war and still advocates for environmental protections and gun control.

'I want to be one of the greatest voices in my generation to affect the things that I want to do to ensure, for example, that children aren't getting slaughtered in classrooms and to make sure that everyone's clean air and clean water,' she said.

Despite her evisceration of the Democrats in her book, she believes that they are on track to trounce the Republicans at the midterms in November.

'It's my job to study the American people and how they feel,' she said. 'They are fuming right now. They are hurting, and I hurt with them.'

For now, Li has stepped back from fundraising, given the lack of a candidate she fully supports. But she is keen to remind the political establishment that she and her rolodex still exist, ready to spring into action.

'I do whatever is right for our country, and I'm waiting for a candidate that I can totally support.

'If I wanted to raise five million dollars I could. I know exactly who to call.
news.summary: As an avowed Democratic Party insider, Lindy Li had a front row seat to the implosion of Biden's campaign for re-election and the ascension of his Vice President Kamala Harris to the ticket.
news.author: Charlotte McDonald-Gibson,Editor

news.title: Heartland Republican calls out 'taxpayer-funded' TV ads in break from Trump
news.text:
Republican congressional candidate Brinker Harding is splitting with the Trump administration regarding its use of taxpayer-funded television campaign advertisements and is stating that Washington should concentrate on those Americans who are having to deal with high costs rather than use public money for political messaging.

“America is $40 trillion dollars in debt, and Nebraskans are struggling to make ends meet. We should be laser focused on spending the taxpayers’ hard earned dollars wisely, not funding political TV advertisements with their money,” Harding said.

“On the Omaha City Council, I balance the city budget every year while ensuring our citizens get the essential services their tax dollars go toward. I will do the same thing in Washington," he added.

Harding is the Republican candidate for Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District, a seat in the Omaha area which is still a competitive district. Although Kamala Harris won the district in the 2024 presidential election, the Republican representative Don Bacon secured re-election with 50.9 per cent of the vote. Bacon is now retiring and is therefore leaving the vacancy to be filled by Harding, who will have to face Democrat Denise Powell and Libertarian Eric Michael Foreman.

The White House is, at the same time, extending a series of television advertisements featuring President Donald Trump, which are funded by the U.S. government.

A 30-second advertisement shown on Fox News and Newsmax displayed images of Trump, highlighted his record on taxes and manufacturing and stated that “America will never be a communist country.” The advertisement included a declaration that it was “Paid for by the U.S. Government,” as reported by The Associated Press.

The White House has described the commercials as public service announcements, stating that they are educational and patriotic and not campaign advertising. Since Trump will not be a candidate in the November election, the advertisements do not directly urge viewers to vote for Republican candidates.

The campaign has come under criticism from members of both political parties. The Republican senator from North Carolina, Thom Tillis, who is not running for re-election, described the advertising as inappropriate, and the Democrats have raised questions as to whether the spending conforms to the federal rules concerning taxpayer-funded publicity or propaganda.

In recent days, the administration has extended the campaign by launching a new advertisement which included footage of Mount Rushmore and extracts from Trump's July 4 speech. According to AdImpact, the amount spent on the first commercial by Friday reached at least $443,000.

Fiscal discipline has been incorporated into Harding's campaign. He stated in a voter guide for the Nebraska Examiner that Congress should cut waste, review the federal programs and return to a more regular budget process.

The fact that he is making his criticism comes while both sides are stressing affordability and household costs in the area in the lead-up to the election on Nov. 3.

news.title: Backlash ensues after the Libertarian Party of New Hampshire calls for assassinations, again
news.text:
The Libertarian Party of New Hampshire is facing backlash after calling for the assassination of “basically every elected Democrat” in the state in a now-deleted X post. 

This wasn’t a first for the LPNH. The group has a history of calling for assassinations of elected officials, and voicing other extreme and divisive rhetoric online that ultimately led to their disaffiliation with the National Libertarian Party. 

In the past, the NHLP has condoned the assassination of Kamala Harris, used its platform to direct homophobic rhetoric at Libertarian presidential nominee Chase Oliver, and openly criticized the national party’s effectiveness. 

The national party cut ties with the LPNH in May, due to the “unfortunate culmination of years of behavior in violation of the Libertarian Party’s platform,” Libertarian National Committee Chair Evan McMahon said in a statement posted on social media. 

The Libertarian Party Judicial Committee later unanimously rejected LPNH’s appeal and the national party now recognizes the Granite State Libertarian Party as its New Hampshire affiliate. 

In a statement regarding LPNH’s most recent statement, the national party said calling for violence goes against the party’s ideals. 

“The Non-Aggression Principle is a fundamental core of libertarianism,” the party said on social media. “It is not optional, and it is central to what our party stands for.”

Many New Hampshire Democrats, and some Republicans, took to social media to voice their disapproval of LPNH’s post. 

“Rhetoric calling for political assassination has no place in New Hampshire or our country — something we should all be able to agree on regardless of our political beliefs,” U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, who is currently running for Senate in New Hampshire, said in a statement. “We work out our differences through the democratic process where we engage in civil debate and seek common ground whenever possible.” 

U.S. Rep Maggie Goodlander called on the New Hampshire Attorney General and federal law enforcement to investigate the threat. 

“I condemn, with every fiber of my being, the threats of and calls for murder from the Libertarian Party of New Hampshire,” she said on social media. “…You can disagree with someone as deeply as humanly possible. But in the United States of America you cannot call for their killing and go unpunished.” 

Lily Tang Williams, a Republican congressional nominee challenging Goodlander, condemned LPNH’s promotion of political violence. 

“Political violence has no place in America — period,” she said in a statement. “As someone who survived an oppressive communist regime where political violence was common, I know we should never take for granted our ability to settle disagreements through free speech, peaceful debate, and elections.” 

Days after the controversial post was made, LPNH chair Jeremy Kauffman posted a screenshot showing that the LPNH account had been temporarily locked for a week or more for breaking X’s rules. 

“It remains a major asymmetry that communists can openly argue for mass enslavement, but patriots cannot advocate for self-defense,” Kauffman said in regards to LPNH’s temporary suspension. 

LPNH said on social media earlier this month it offered to turn over all of its assets to the Granite State Libertarian Party, including its social media account, but the offer was rejected by the national party. 

The national Libertarian party leadership team said it is “reviewing all legal options to protect the Party’s brand of freedom, peace, and prosperity,” according to the Boston Globe.
news.summary:
The group's prior divisive rhetoric ultimately led to their disaffiliation with the National Libertarian Party.
