news.title: Trump and GOP See Reversal With Latinos in 2 Strongholds Ahead of Midterms
news.text: Hispanic voters in South Texas and South Florida are showing signs of moving away from President Donald Trump and the Republican Party, just five weeks before the midterm elections. The two regions were key to Trump's gains with Latino voters in 2024, when he made major inroads in heavily Hispanic areas of both states. Now, Republican-held House seats in South Texas and South Florida are becoming more competitive, while the Texas U.S. Senate race has also tightened. For Democrats, the shift has raised hopes of winning a statewide election in Texas for the first time since 1994. The Cook Political Report, widely considered the industry standard for nonpartisan race ratings, moved three Florida House races and three Texas House races toward Democrats, including Texas' 9th Congressional District, which had long been considered solidly Republican. While the two electorates are different, political strategists who track Latino voters told Newsweek they are responding to many of the same concerns. The Latino Problem for the GOP in Texas A survey of Hispanic likely voters in Texas conducted for the Cook Political Report and TelevisaUnivision found Trump's job approval at 33 percent, two years after he carried Texas Hispanics by 10 percentage points. Republican Senator Ted Cruz won the group by 3 points in 2024. Texas state Representative James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, leads Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton 63 percent to 30 percent among Hispanic voters, including 73 percent of self-described independents. In the governor's race, Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa leads Republican Governor Greg Abbott 60 percent to 33 percent. Abbott won 40 percent of Hispanics in 2022. Much of the movement comes from Trump voters. Eighteen percent of Texas Hispanics who backed him in 2024 disapprove of his performance, 19 percent support Talarico over Paxton and 22 percent do not back a Republican in a generic House matchup. Mike Madrid, a longtime Republican strategist and author of The Latino Century, said Washington misread what happened in 2024. "People, I think, broadly are failing to understand that the Latino vote is the largest swing vote in America," Madrid told Newsweek. "Most people were thinking it was part of this permanent realignment. A lot of people who understand the Latino vote were saying it's not that at all." Immigration enforcement is also a drag. Nearly two-thirds of respondents said they would be less likely to vote for a candidate who supports Trump's deportation policy, and 61 percent view Immigration and Customs Enforcement unfavorably. Voters still ranked the economy as their top concern by roughly 2-to-1 over immigration. Every public poll of the race conducted in September has shown Talarico ahead, most within the margin of error. Newsweek reached out to the Paxton and Talarico campaigns for comment Monday. South Texas House Races Tighten as Latino Voters Shift On September 25, Cook moved three Texas House races toward Democrats: the 15th District from Lean Republican to Toss-Up, the 35th from Likely Republican to Lean Republican, and the 9th from Solid Republican to Likely Republican. Only the 15th is in the Rio Grande Valley, though Cook's poll also sampled voters in the Democratic-held 28th and 34th districts, both of which Texas Republicans redrew last year to make them more favorable to the GOP. But the pressure is visible there. Bobby Pulido, a Tejano singer with two Latin Grammy Awards and broad name recognition across South Texas, is challenging Republican Representative Monica De La Cruz in a district Trump won by 18 points in 2024. A Texas Southern University poll puts Pulido ahead 50 percent to 45 percent. Madrid, who recently traveled to South Texas, said voters there described specific grievances. He pointed to the administration's moves on Argentine beef in a region built on ranching. "This is cattle-ranching country," he said. "He's literally poking the stick in the eye of fifth-generation Hispanic cattle ranchers. It's not like an academic discussion or a debate. He's directly attacking their businesses." In the 28th District, Democratic Representative Henry Cuellar faces Tano Tijerina, a Webb County judge who switched from Democrat to Republican and won the GOP primary decisively. Trump won the district by 10 points under the new map. Cook rated the race Lean Democratic after Trump's pardon in December 2025 ended the federal bribery case against Cuellar. Coverage in recent months has focused on the race tightening, with Trump criticizing Cuellar while openly backing Tijerina. The 34th District, which covers the Brownsville-McAllen area, is also roughly Trump +10 under the new lines. There, Democratic Representative Vicente Gonzalez faces Republican Eric Flores, a former assistant U.S. attorney. No independent general-election poll of the race has been published. An NRCC poll in late April had Flores ahead 41 percent to 40 percent, and a mid-June Ragnar Research poll had him up 44 percent to 41 percent. Cook and Sabato's Crystal Ball rate it a Toss-Up. What Polling Shows in the Florida Races After Cook's Shift If any place has rewarded the Republican Party, and Trump in particular, for courting Hispanic voters, it is South Florida. In 2016, Hillary Clinton won Miami-Dade County by 29 points. Four years later, Joe Biden carried it by just 7. In 2024, Trump became the first Republican presidential candidate since 1988 to win the county, where roughly 71 percent of the 2.8 million residents are Hispanic. He beat Kamala Harris there by 11 points, and an NBC exit poll found that he won 58 percent of the Latino vote statewide. The shift was built largely on Cuban and Venezuelan American voters, many of whom fled leftist governments and have long seen the GOP as their political home. Those are the voters Republicans now risk losing. On September 25, Cook moved three Florida House races toward Democrats: the 27th and 13th districts from Likely Republican to Lean Republican, and the 22nd from Lean Republican to Toss-Up. Republican Representative Maria Elvira Salazar's 27th District, which covers Miami, Coral Gables, Palmetto Bay and Cutler Bay, is the one most tied to Latino voters. Almost three in four residents are Latino. Cook cited recent polls and a Hispanic backlash against the Trump administration that it said forced Salazar to play defense. The race has escalated in recent days. After Salazar's ad criticizing Trump's immigration enforcement, the president shared at least 14 posts from other users attacking her on Truth Social. She has not directly responded to his weekend posts. Newsweek reached out to Salazar for comment Monday. An internal poll for her Democratic challenger, former CBS Miami anchor Eliott Rodriguez, found the two tied at 45 percent once undecided voters were asked. The same survey found Trump 10 points underwater in the district, with 54 percent disapproving of his job performance. Forty-four percent said Salazar deserves reelection, and 47 percent said they would prefer someone new. The poll was conducted by Bendixen & Amandi International, which works for Rodriguez's campaign. Eduardo Gamarra, a political science professor at Florida International University who publishes a weekly tracking report on the Latino vote in Florida, told Newsweek that his report had flagged Salazar's district as competitive for the first time this cycle. "I live there. I'm already seeing a lot more negative commentary about her online than I was a week ago," he said. The newly drawn 22nd District stretches across parts of western Broward and Palm Beach counties and includes Hendry and Collier counties. The old district backed Trump 55 percent to 44 percent in 2024 after voting for Joe Biden 51 percent to 48 percent in 2020. Democrat Pia Dandiya is running against Republican Casey Askar. In the Tampa Bay-area 13th District, Democrat Leela Gray leads Republican Representative Anna Paulina Luna 51 percent to 46 percent in a House Majority PAC poll conducted by Hart Research Associates. An internal poll conducted for Luna by Fabrizio, Lee & Associates in August showed her leading by 8 points, a sign of how much the race has shifted in recent polling. What Other Polls Say About Latino Voters Other surveys point the same direction. A Pew Research Center survey in April found that 66 percent of Latino Trump voters approve of his job performance, down 27 percentage points since the start of his second term in January 2025. A New York Times/Siena poll conducted September 8-13 places Trump's approval among Hispanic voters at 26 percent. In Texas, a separate UnidosUS poll found that 54 percent of Latino voters surveyed across five competitive districts planned to support the Democratic candidate, compared with 27 percent for the Republican. The same polls carry warnings for Democrats. Texas Hispanic voters in the Cook survey preferred Republican messaging on transgender athletes over a progressive alternative by more than 20 points, though few named it as a top issue. In Florida, the UnidosUS poll found that dissatisfaction with Trump is not translating into support for Democratic candidates in the two marquee races on the statewide ballot. Among Hispanic voters in Florida, Republican Senator Ashley Moody led Democratic state Representative Angie Nixon 40 percent to 32 percent, while in the governor's race, Republican Representative Byron Donalds led Democrat David Jolly, a former GOP congressman, 40 percent to 33 percent. More than one-quarter of respondents were undecided in each race. "This is 100 percent about the Republicans," Madrid told Newsweek. "Not that the Democrats are doing anything right. It's that the Republicans are doing everything wrong." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Hispanic voters in South Texas and South Florida are showing signs of moving away from President Donald Trump.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: Kamala Harris Brutally Mocked as Ex-Veep Hits Midterm Campaign Trail — as Critics Say She's 'Still Giving a Word Salad Answer for Everything
news.text:
Democrats in Michigan have little enthusiasm for former Vice President Kamala Harris and her "word salad," with some critics saying, once more, that she comes off as confusing or insincere, RadarOnline can report.

Harris is making stops in key midterm battlegrounds, including an appearance in Michigan alongside Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.Kamala Harris' Latest 'Word Salad'She is also scheduled to campaign for Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Nevada gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford.

At a maternal and infant health center, Harris spoke about what "black people and black birthing people need in order to move themselves forward." She linked attacks on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) to threats against maternal care for Black women.

"[An attack on DEI] is an attack by definition on maternal care, including the need to protect Black women in connection with their pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum care," Harris said.

The connection between the two topics was not explained, prompting one anonymous Democratic operative to tell The New York Post she was saying "a whole lot of word salad."Kamala Harris Making a Comeback?Harris has not decided whether she will run for president in 2028, but her midterm activity is fueling speculation that she is keeping the option open. 

The Associated Press reported that she is actively campaigning for Democratic candidates in Michigan, Nevada and Georgia as she considers a potential 2028 bid.

As Radar previously reported, Gov. Gavin Newsom is also being discussed as a potential 2028 candidate. Her name remains prominent in early 2028 Democratic preference polling. 

The RealClearPolitics average through September 21 has Harris at 24.9 percent, followed by Newsom at 14 percent, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 12.8 percent, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at 10.7 percent.Kansas Dem Candidate's Plea to Kamala Harris: 'Don’t Come'Meanwhile, some Democrats have questioned her value as a surrogate. 

Kansas Senate candidate Pastor Adam Hamilton said on State of Play with Peter Alexander on September 23 that Harris would not help his campaign and preferred she stay away.

Hamilton said he and Harris are ideologically different and argued that her appearance could hurt his chances with undecided voters and Republicans who are frustrated with President Trump's policies and could be considering voting Democratic.

"No offense intended for her, but she would not be a help to me," Hamilton told Alexander. "We are a different kind of Democrat, and the national Democrats, some of the leaders, do not represent where the people in Kansas are."Old GaffesHarris' choice of words and phrases has drawn criticism throughout her vice presidency and her 2024 presidential campaign.

One of the most memorable lines from her 2024 campaign came in Pittsburgh on September 2, 2024, when she said, "We have dreams. We can see what is possible, unburdened by what has been. We have aspirations. We have ambitions, and the system that is a good system is one that supports that and allows people the opportunity to go where they can see and imagine themselves to be."

In a January 2022 interview with NBC's Today, Harris was asked whether it was time to change the Biden administration’s COVID-19 strategy.

"It is time for us to do what we have been doing. And that time is every day," she said before discussing efforts to slow the spread of the virus.

On August 2, 2024, while discussing a prisoner exchange that brought three detained Americans home from Russia, Harris said on CNN it was "an extraordinary testament to the importance of having a president who understands the power of diplomacy and understands the strength that rests in understanding the significance of diplomacy and strengthening alliances."
news.summary: Kamala Harris faces renewed criticism over her speaking style as she returns to the midterm campaign trail for Democratic candidates in Michigan, Georgia and Nevada.

news.title: Rocker Michael Stipe Holding Major NYC Fundraiser for Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed
news.text:
R.E.M. frontman Michael Stipe is set to help host a massive fundraiser in Manhattan for Michigan Democrat U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, reports say.

The big event will be held on the Bowery on October 5, an advanced flyer for the fundraiser notes, according to the New York Post.

Stipe will be joined by New York jeweler Alexis Bittar, Democrat House candidate Brad Lander, ex-Congressman Jamaal Bowman, and Brooklyn Councilman Chi Osse.

Socialist New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s close campaign aides, political strategists Andrew Bard Esptein and Zara Rahim, are also members of the hosting group.

Bard Esptein reportedly told the media that he has joined the El-Sayed event because the Michigan Democrat is a “candidate I believe in.”

Tickets cost from between $250 for the lowest level to $57,800 for the top tier of donors.

The flyer works to take the edge off El-Sayed Muslim and radical left-wing background by calling him a “Michigan native running to make government work for ALL of us.”

R.E.M.’s Stipe has stumped for far-left candidates in the past. Back in 2016, for instance, he campaigned for socialist U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders in his last losing campaign for the Democrat nomination for president.

He also supported Kamala Harris in 2024 and was one of many in the entertainment industry to urge Joe Biden to step down from running against Donald Trump that year.

news.text:
Democrat Adam Hamilton, who is running for the U.S. Senate in Kansas, has been exposed as a woke megachurch pastor who preaches on issues like Black Lives Matter, environmentalism, and the radical LGBTQ agenda. He went so far as to say in a June 2020 sermon that, "By virtue of being white,I have to repent."

Hamilton knows his radical agenda won't play well with Kansas voters, and he even told former Vice President Kamala Harris to stay away from his campaign. "Please do not come to my state," Hamilton said in an MSNOW interview. "I do not need you here. You would actually hurt me."

But Hamilton is doing a good job of hurting his own campaign, which was recently caught lying about his Republican opponent, Roger Marshall. The Hamilton campaign dropped an ad claiming Marshall had a woman arrested over a missed $50 medical payment.

#KSSen: D candidate Adam Hamilton is up on TV with this spot --Meischa to camera:"One evening I see lights. I open the door and it's a police officer. They arrested me because I didn't make a $50 payment to Roger Marshall" pic.twitter.com/o5x7WkXLGp— Medium Buying (@MediumBuying) September 25, 2026

"One evening, I see lights. I open the door and it's a police officer," says a woman named Meischa. "They arrested me because I didn't make a $50 payment to Roger Marshall. I was eight months pregnant and I said 'Please, do not handcuff me in front of my two-year-old daughter.' Roger Marshall preyed on the low-income families of Kansas. The healthcare system is broken, but not for Roger Marshall. He's absolutely profiting from it."

But this ad is a lie. Meischa was not arrested for a missed payment on a medical debt. The Kansas Bill of Rights (Section 16) explicitly prohibits imprisonment for debt. No one in Kansas can be arrested and jailed for failing to pay a bill.

The reality is that a judge ordered Meischa's arrest after she failed to appear in court more than 16 times over a three-year period, and court records show she has a history of failing to appear in court.

“Meischa received notices to appear in court and ignored them.” pic.twitter.com/Ed9XxQtdhO— Shay (@Shaykcprincess) September 25, 2026

Even the $50 debt was a lie. Heartland Regional sought more than $3,500 from Meischa and sent that amount to collections. The $50 bill was owed to Hutch Clinic, a different hospital and a different doctor — not Roger Marshall.

It's also untrue that Meischa was "surprised" by the arrest. She has been called to court by eight different businesses in three different Kansas counties over a multi-year period, including a different hospital and an eviction.

The Hamilton campaign knows his radical agenda won't play well with Kansas voters, so instead he's using scaremongering and dishonest ads to deceive voters. Telling voters that Marshall had a pregnant woman arrested because she didn't make a $50 payment just isn't true. The actual debt was thousands of dollars, the $50 debt was for a different hospital and different doctor, and the arrest came after Meischa repeatedly failed to appear in court.

If Hamilton wants Kansas voters to trust him with a seat in the Senate, his campaign should do better than this.

news.title: Data Center Party Dared Critics To ‘Come And Take It.’ A Few Tried And Failed
news.text:
WASHINGTON — A celebration of data centers kept humming Saturday night despite protesters’ best attempts to take over the stage.

Four protesters took the stage during the toasts and remarks at Data After Dark, a pro-data center party at the Washington, D.C. bar PubKey. The event, organized by Pirate Wires reporter Jonas Du, R Street Institute tech fellow Ed Tarnowski and Young Voices CEO Casey Given, drew hundreds of attendees who chanted “USA” as protesters were ushered out of the venue.

Asked why he opposed data centers, the first protester told the DCNF, “I wanna live,” as security rushed him out of the bar. “Our only fucking home [planet Earth]. Just so you can get rich. It’s despicable. It’s fucking despicable.” 

Daily Caller News Foundation / Screenshot

Among the other protesters was a woman who flipped off the crowd as their chants drowned out her declarations. “Thank you for using all of our water. You are killing the world” the woman yelled through the noise, according to another angle of the incident posted Sunday on X. 

Several protesters just interrupted the pro-data center party, flipped everyone off while yelling “thank you for using all of our water!” pic.twitter.com/UlyjxJAKIt— philip lewis (@Phil_Lewis_) September 27, 2026

“How is this ‘USA’?” she asked as the crowd chanted. 

“Fuck all of you,” she said as she raised her middle fingers to the audience. 

Two other women then interrupted the speakers’ remarks before security forcibly removed them from the stage. (RELATED: Anti-Data Center Group Planned Massive ‘Revolt.’ Barely A Soul Showed Up)

Protesters crashed the @JonasYDu pro-data center party tonight. One flipped off the crowd. None could be heard over shouts of “USA” and booing. pic.twitter.com/HIjnN9nSED— Natalie Sandoval (@NatSandovalDC) September 27, 2026

“I started a ‘USA’ chant to drown them out,” Matt Kita, a Bitcoin investor who attended the event, said in an early Sunday X post. “We will re-industrialize and we will win.”

Thank you @JonasYDu for a great night at @PubKey in DC.I can confirm doomer nerds stormed the stage. I can also confirm I started a “USA” chant to drown them out. We will re-industrialize and we will win. https://t.co/RRltjgi5nQ— matt kita (@mattkita) September 27, 2026

R Street Institute analyst Adam Thierer spoke after the protesters rushed the stage, and he said the debate over data centers comes down to “makers or takers.”

“Well, we know who doesn’t believe in freedom, it’s the kind of freaks who were just up here charging the stage.” Thierer said. 

The data center debate is “a fight between those of us who believe in prosperity and permissionless innovation versus those who believe in poisonous, parasitic thinking,” he argued.

‘Blabbering Some Nonsense’

Du told the DCNF that organizers expected disruption at an event of that size.

“No one could hear what they were saying. They were blabbering some nonsense,” Du said. “I do think we were surprised by how quickly the crowd drowned them out.”

The chant reflected the stakes of the AI race, he argued.

“If we let China win the AI race, for instance, that’s much more of a threat,” Du told the DCNF. “I think that’s why people broke out into the USA chants when the protesters were running onto the stage.”

After the toasts ended, another member of the protest group approached him near the stage and warned that they would disrupt future events, Du said.

“He said, ‘Any future events you throw, we’re gonna be there. We’re gonna disrupt it. Be prepared. We’re coming for you,’” Du recalled. “I laughed him off.”

Daily Caller News Foundation / Screenshot

Du described the opposition to data centers as “slopulism,” which he defined as populist anger over “the thing of the moment” that is easy to stir up, just as low-effort “AI slop” is easy to produce. 

“It’s very, very easy to get people in a room and convince them that data centers are bad because you can just exaggerate all of the harms and talk about none of the good sides and then capitalize on people’s pre-existing fears,” Du said. “If you want to do the opposite thing, that is much harder to do. Which is why it’s called slopulism, because it’s easy.”

‘The Swamp Loves Them’

Data center critics were unmoved by the party.

“D.C., which Kamala Harris won with more than 90% of the vote, is exactly where I’d expect a bunch of tech grifters to gather and celebrate forcing data centers on rural America,” Amy Kremer, chair of Humans First, said in a statement to the DCNF. 

Daily Caller News Foundation / Screenshot

“Meanwhile, this same week, Frederick County, Virginia — a county Trump won by 30 points — voted to ban new data centers. That speaks volumes,” Kremer added. “Rural America hates them. The swamp loves them.”

Frederick County became the first locality in Virginia to ban new data centers when its supervisors voted 6-1 on Wednesday to bar them countywide, according to the Winchester Gazette. 

Du called Kremer’s framing “pretty obvious cherry-picking.”

“I think it’s very lazy for them to try to frame this as a Kamala Harris versus Donald Trump situation,” Du said. “This is where AI policy is going to be formed.”

Du said attendees included people who worked for the Trump administration as well as staffers for Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna of California. The DCNF spoke with both Khanna staffers and a White House official at the party. 

Given, whose group handled logistics after the party outgrew the original venue, told the DCNF ahead of the event that its popularity reflected a side of the debate that rarely gets heard.

“One side of this argument has been tremendously loud and really kind of hysterical, and so I think there’s kind of a quiet, silent majority, if you will, that really don’t have a channel to let their voice out because you have everyone screaming about killer robots, essentially,” Given said.

“[W]hat I’m hoping to accomplish is just to showcase that [the pro-data center side] is a movement, and that really one side of the conversation does not dominate everything,” he added. “There is a different side of the argument, and we’re more fun.”

Daily Caller News Foundation / Screenshot

‘The Polling Is Very Clear’

Other critics argued the turnout does not reflect public opinion.

“I don’t think a party in D.C. changes the fact that data centers are extremely unpopular,” Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of the Alliance for Secure AI, told the DCNF.

“AI is not polling much better these days. [G]iven the news over the past few days, I doubt this will change anytime soon,” he added.

Du acknowledged that data center supporters face an uphill battle. 

“Data centers are still broadly unpopular with the American public. The polling is very clear,” Du said, adding that the party was “an organizing opportunity” amid “the PR [public relations] crisis that the tech industry finds itself in right now.”

Fifty-four percent of U.S. adults said “data centers are mostly bad for the environment,” up from 39 percent in January. Similarly, 50 percent said they are “mostly bad for home energy costs,” an increase from 38 percent in January, according to Pew Research data released Sept. 22.

Meanwhile, just 7 percent of registered voters ranked data centers as a top-three national issue, according to a Sept. 10-14 Rainey Center poll of 1,004 registered voters. AI ranked a top-three issue for 12 percent of voters. 

Only 11 percent of 1,000 respondents said they would support an AI data center being built in their community, and 65 percent opposed it, according to a University of Massachusetts Amherst poll released Sept. 14. 

An NBC News poll of 7,105 American adults, conducted Aug. 20-Sept. 1, similarly found that 69 percent opposed data center construction in their community while 31 percent supported it. 

Given said some local concerns, including zoning, water and electricity, are “perfectly reasonable,” but argued they can be addressed “through the processes of democracy” and that the benefits of data centers outweigh the costs.

“The conversation should be that yes, AI is good, data centers are good. We definitely need guardrails, as we do with everything in life,” Given said. 

‘Really, It’s A Competition’

The original idea for the event was a small house party before the event went viral online, Du told the DCNF. More than 1,000 people were added to the guest list for the event on Partiful, about 600 of whom attended over the course of the evening, Du said. 

A long line formed outside PubKey as the event began, according to a photo posted on X. At its peak, the line wrapped around the block, Du said. 

Crazy queue! 🕺 https://t.co/tOjDS9aSCB pic.twitter.com/anvHI8Lcyv— Reem Ibrahim (@ReemAmirIbrahim) September 27, 2026

The event was presented by Pirate Wires, Young Voices and Compute Optimist and sponsored by several additional groups, such as the Manhattan Institute, NetChoice, the Bitcoin Policy Institute and the ’76 Crew, according to Du’s Saturday X post.

The party featured an AI photo booth, a DJ, a jazz trio and themed cocktails. 

The names of the drinks were meant to highlight arguments for data centers, according to Tarnowski’s Sunday X post. The “SMR-tini” nodded to small nuclear reactors that can power data centers, the “Closed Loop Spritz” to water-recycling cooling systems and the “Loudoun County Iced Tea” to Northern Virginia’s “Data Center Alley.”

A photo of the drink menu was posted on X during the event.

Can’t wait for my Loudoun County Iced Tea tonight!🍹 pic.twitter.com/qh3T621sFJ— Reem Ibrahim (@ReemAmirIbrahim) September 26, 2026

 A similar event, “AI After Dark: Party - #SFTechWeek” is scheduled for Oct. 9 in San Francisco, CA, on Partiful. 

“We want to bring this to other cities across the nation because I think that you need to bring the same level of energy that the anti-data center people are bringing to this issue,” Du said. “Really, it’s a competition.”
news.summary: ‘F*ck all of you’

news.title: America, the ‘arsenal of democracy,’ is now disarming the press
news.text:
By Lionel Barber 

In a radio address in December 1940, one year before the US entered World War II, Franklin D Roosevelt described America as “the arsenal of democracy”. Today, the guns are falling silent across the western front. Independent journalism, the lifeblood of an informed democracy, faces existential challenges, particularly in the US.

The threats are economic and technological, but they are also legal and political in nature. The second Trump administration is targeting news organisations aggressively, filing multi-billion law suits, hunting down sources through subpoenas, and waging a campaign of vilification against any reporter or editor who fails to toe the line.

There is scant precedent for this abuse of executive power. Not even Richard Nixon at the height of the Watergate scandal comes close.

The assault on independent journalism is being mounted – in plain sight – using the awesome power of the Federal government.

The courts, the last line of defence, have so far stood firm; but no one can be sure where the US Supreme Court, with its in-built long-term conservative majority, will come down in the final instance, should things head that way.

The bedrock Supreme Court decision defending freedom of the press in the US is New York Times Co v Sullivan (1964) which established that public officials cannot sue for defamation unless they prove “actual malice” – that is to say, the publisher knew the information was false or acted with reckless disregard.

A second foundational case is New York Times Co v United States (1971) – the so-called Pentagon Papers case in which the Court heavily restricted the government’s ability to exercise prior restraint or block the publication of classified defence information.

In both cases, the Supreme Court rulings set a high bar for the government to muzzle the media. But these enlightened rulings are relics of a bygone era. The Sixties and Seventies were marked by a profound distrust of the Federal government, exacerbated by the Vietnam War. The media’s exposure of the government’s lies used to justify the prosecution of that war lent newspapers, radio and television a new legitimacy.

Half a century on, public cynicism has spread to the media itself. Journalists rank below lawyers and estate agents, according to some surveys. Some of the mistrust may have been earned as a result of missteps and overreach; but that is the price of a free press. Today, when social media algorithms prioritise engagement which in turn rewards conflict and outrage, established news organisations find themselves branded as biased and disreputable.

The Trump administration has been the most aggressive proponent and litigant in this media intimidation campaign.

In 2024, the Walt Disney Co agreed to pay $15m to the Trump presidential library and pay $1m in legal fees to settle a defamation suit brought against Disney’s ABC News subsidiary. Disney settled after its star anchor – former Clinton administration communications director George Stephanopoulos – said Trump had been found “liable for rape”. (A New York judge had ruled that Trump was liable for “sexual assault”).

In 2025, Paramount agreed to pay the Trump presidential library $16m to settle a legal dispute over the editing of a CBS news programme featuring an interview with then Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump claimed the edit “tipped the scales” against him in the 2024 presidential campaign – despite the fact that he ended up a clear winner against Democratic candidate Harris.

Though Paramount admitted no guilt, it preferred to settle at a time when it needed the Federal government’s blessing for its planned multi-billion dollar merger with Skydance Media. Similarly, Walt Disney calculated that it was not worth testing a reasonable defence in court highlighting the fact that Trump’s notoriety made him a libel-proof plaintiff. In short, corporate interest has taken precedence over the constitutional principle of the freedom of the press.

There are noble exceptions. The New York Times, Wall Street Journal and the BBC have declined to settle multi-billion dollar lawsuits filed by President Trump. Indeed, the New York Times is suing the Pentagon over its decision to restrict access to reporters. The BBC is also contesting a $10bn defamation claim over a documentary on the January 6th riots. The case is due to be heard in a Florida court next year.

It is tempting to dismiss these fears as the product of a fevered liberal imagination. But I have been visiting the US regularly for the past 50 years. I was stationed as a foreign correspondent for the Financial Times for a decade, first in Washington and later in New York. I know the country (47 states and counting) and I consider dozens of American journalists to be personal friends. The threats to news organisations, large and small, constitute a clear and present danger.

America is the land of the First Amendment which guarantees freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly and the right to petition the government. What happens in Washington does not stay in Washington. If America falls short in upholding the constitutional principle of a free press, others will act with greater impunity. The world will be a far darker place.

Lionel Barber is an English journalist and former editor of the Financial Times. Until recently he was the co-host of the podcast Media Confidential.

This article was commissioned to mark World News Day, a worldwide campaign highlighting the essential role of journalism in providing facts and clarity.
news.summary:
In a radio address in December 1940, one year before the US entered World War II, Franklin D Roosevelt described America as “the arsenal of democracy”. Today, the guns are falling silent across the western front. Independent journalism, the lifeblood of an informed democracy, faces existential challenges, particularly in the US, writes Lionel Barber for World News Day.

news.title: 'Lower 48' is a phrase to fight over in Alaska. It's a fixture in the state's U.S. Senate contest
news.text: One of the most biting insults in Alaska politics is to be accused of being aligned with the “Lower 48," code for candidates taking marching orders from powerful forces in the contiguous United States rather than sticking up for Alaskans. It's a central theme of the Alaska's U.S. Senate race, one of a handful expected to determine control of the chamber in the November elections. Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan's campaign has made it a key attack line against Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman. He lumps her in with “Lower 48 liberals” who have opposed expanded oil and gas drilling in a state that has relied heavily on that industry for decades. Peltola, an Alaska Native, has countered that she “took on” then-President Biden, a fellow Democrat, to help win approval in 2023 of the huge Willow oil project, which environmentalists strongly opposed. She also says she will “take on anyone, including Democrats — anyone in the Lower 48 who doesn’t understand what Alaska needs.” The pejorative label reflects a mystique about Alaska, which outsiders often refer to as “The Last Frontier." A state for less than 70 years, Alaska is renowned for its natural beauty, wildlife and vast landscapes. Its rural nature — isolated from the rest of the country and with many of its communities accessible only by air or water — breeds a self-reliance. It's a place where many residents hunt and fish to fill their freezers for winter and take pride in their independence. The two major Senate campaigns and some third-party groups have leaned into that sentiment — that Alaska is different — and cast their candidates as authentic voices for Alaskans. “We love the persona Alaska is a tough place to live," said Republican Andrew Halcro, a political podcast host and former state lawmaker who has lived in the state nearly all his life. Alaska, rich in natural resources, has long had a love-hate relationship with the federal government, which owns about 60% of the state's land. That relationship has been especially strained under Democratic presidential administrations that have sought to restrict logging, mining and the availability of areas for oil and gas development over environmental concerns. Policies can shift dramatically from one administration to the next. The Democratic Obama and Biden administrations banned leasing on roughly half the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska, which is home to wildlife such as caribou and polar bears and provides habitat for millions of migrating birds. Republican President Trump's administration has rolled back those and other restrictions as part of a broader push for expanded oil and gas development in Alaska. The administration also is supporting lease sales in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. The state also has bristled at Democratic efforts to stifle road building and logging in areas such as the Tongass National Forest, a temperate rainforest in southeast Alaska. That dispute dates to the Clinton administration. Alaska's share of royalty revenue from oil and minerals on federal land has been another ongoing source of tension. Some lawmakers say the state was promised a larger share at statehood and that the federal government has failed to uphold its end of the deal. While oil production is a fraction of what it was at its peak in the late 1980s and has fallen in recent years, political leaders have pointed to signs of a turnaround. They cite in part the strong interest from major companies that snatched up leases in a sale earlier this year for the petroleum reserve, home to the Willow project. Alaska communities have been hit hard by spikes in fuel prices caused by the Iran war. That is especially true for remote communities that must have their fuel flown in or delivered by barge before the rivers ice over. Oil development is the top issue in this year's election for Darryl Hugo, who lives in the small North Slope community of Anaktuvuk Pass. He is backing Sullivan and notes that revenue from oil development is largely responsible for his town's health clinic, school, police and fire departments and water system. “My region’s economy depends on oil,” he said via a messaging app. Robert Sewell, an independent from the Juneau area, said he sees the “Lower 48” taunts and Peltola trying to distance herself from national Democrats as examples of the candidates “fighting to establish who is the real spokesperson for the real Alaska.” He also likens it a bit to the schoolyard jeer, “I know you are, but what am I?” Peltola, during her unsuccessful 2024 congressional reelection campaign, refused to endorse Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris and said she would not vote for Trump. This year, before Alaska's August primary, Harris sent a fundraising appeal that offered support of Peltola. In response, Peltola's campaign told reporters that she “isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48.” In videos highlighting her backing of the Willow oil project, Peltola said she will work with Trump, who handily carried Alaska each of the three times he has run, to advance more oil and gas projects. “I took on Joe Biden to secure the largest development project in decades,” she said in one video on social media. “And I’ll work with Donald Trump on more.” Sewell, a Peltola supporter, said he does not begrudge that position. He said he does not think "for one moment that she likes Trump or Trump’s agendas" on other issues. Peltola, who is Yup’ik, is among the roughly 43% of Alaskans born in the state. She grew up fishing on the Kuskokwim River in western Alaska and prominently displays fishing photos on her website. Her campaign slogan, “Fish, Family, Freedom,” is intended to appeal to what she believes are Alaskans' shared values. Sullivan, originally from Ohio, came to Alaska in the late 1990s when he was in his early 30s. Now a retired Marine, he served as Alaska attorney general and natural resources commissioner, and was an assistant secretary of state in President George W. Bush's administration. Sullivan spokesperson Nate Adams said that for the senator, “being an Alaskan means loving this state, fighting everyday for his fellow Alaskans and making sure Alaskans, not Lower 48 liberals, decide our future.” The SLF PAC, which supports a Republican Senate majority, has been keying in on that theme. In one of its ads, a speaker says of Peltola, “They dress her up, throw her out on a stream somewhere, make her look like an Alaskan.” Another says: “Mary Peltola sounds like Alaska, but toes a different line in Washington, D.C.” Peltola's campaign said Alaskans “won’t be fooled by mudslinging ads.” In a statement, her campaign sought to link Sullivan with “Lower 48 special interest donors.” Halcro, the former lawmaker and podcaster, said Alaskans have been inundated with such ads and flyers, but he is not sure the messaging over which candidate aligns less with the “Lower 48” is one voters want to hear this year. “It's all of this stuff just to make us angry at a time where we really genuinely, genuinely just need stability,” he said. “We just need to elect somebody who’s not going to break anything.” Bohrer writes for the Associated Press.
news.summary: The most biting insult in Alaska politics is to be accused of being aligned with the “Lower 48." The pejorative label reflects a mystique about Alaska, which outsiders often refer to as “The Last Frontier."
news.author: Becky Bohrer

news.title: Madonna Understands the Trump Rule of Power
news.text: Madonna opened the increasingly, almost traumatically, passé MTV Video Music Awards on Sunday night surrounded by women young enough to have grown up in a world she had already remade. There was Sabrina Carpenter, 27, singing "Bring Your Love," the collaboration from Madonna’s Confessions II. Then came Charli XCX, 34, emerging from a bathroom stall for "Danceteria Afterhours," followed by a small parade of cameos that included Julia Garner, Debi Mazar, Sombr and Seth Rogen. It was Madonna’s first VMA performance in 23 years and Madonna, 68, was certainly still Madonna. The "Queen of Pop" wore the corset and thigh-high boots that have come to define both her onstage and offstage personas. There were also bondage-clad dancers that worked well with the old mixture of sex, spectacle and provocation that Madonna is associated with. There are many ways to read a 68-year-old pop star returning to a stage she helped make culturally important. Nostalgia is the easiest and another go-to would be vanity, but Madonna offered a more interesting possibility: perhaps longevity begins with declining to cooperate with other people’s timetable for your disappearance. It is a rule President Donald Trump appears to understand unusually well but that Madonna learned first. Later that night, while accepting the VMA for Artist of the Year, Madonna told a story about the first time she performed at the awards, back in 1984. During "Like a Virgin," one of her stilettos came off so she dove after it and, as she moved through the air, her dress went up and her derriere was exposed. According to her own retelling, Madonna went backstage rather pleased with herself. Her manager’s assistant had a different assessment: her "career was over." This is funny now for obvious reasons: Madonna went on to become one of the defining pop stars of the next four decades. But there is something else in the story that explains Sunday night better than any corset could. Madonna has been being told she is over almost as long as she has been Madonna. At first, she was too vulgar. Then too controversial. Eventually, inevitably, she became too old. Pop music kept producing replacements and Madonna kept encountering them, collaborating with them, kissing them, competing with them and occasionally collecting awards alongside them. Case in point: all of last night. Madonna doesn't want to be the building block on which the Taylor Swifts and Sabrina Carpenters of the world build their careers. She intends to keep building her own tower alongside them. Madonna showed generations of women what a female pop star could be, but she has never seemed particularly interested in showing them how a female pop star gracefully leaves. Whether we approve of that, or whether it ends up reinforcing exactly the kind of feminism many people reject—the idea that a woman remains relevant only so long as she can remain young—is almost beside the point. Madonna seems to be asking a different question: Why, exactly, should Madonna help us replace Madonna? She does not want to be the former Queen of Pop. She wants to be the current Queen of Pop, perennially, forever, everlastingly, almost defiantly unaging. It is a kind of mental pyrotechnic remarkably close to the way Trump understands power—which is especially ironic considering how loudly Madonna has opposed him for years. The comparison between Madonna and Trump is not a political one. It’s clear that the powers of a pop star and a president aren’t comparable, even though Trump has made it clear he is a cultural phenomenon and wants to be treated as a celebrity, and the celebrity world has come to show that chiming in on politics is now part of their job. But moving past that, what Trump and Madonna share is an acute understanding of the theater surrounding power: people can tell you that your era has ended and institutions can prep for who is next—heck, the entire culture can start speaking about you in the past tense…but you are under no obligation to join them. Trump demonstrated the principle after 2020 with considerably greater consequences. He lost the election, left the White House and then declined to assume the cultural role America normally assigns former presidents. Four years later, he defeated Kamala Harris, winning the Electoral College 312-226, and returned to the White House as the 47th president. At the very least, we can admit that, by the terms of his own playbook, something worked: he refused to behave like a man whose political moment had passed, and eventually the presidency was his again. Whatever else Trump’s return means, it established a useful distinction about power: losing it and agreeing that your time is over are two different things. Madonna has mastered that move. At 68, she was back at the VMAs performing with women born after some of her most famous performances, dressed recognizably as herself and later accepting Artist of the Year. She won seven awards Sunday night. Perhaps there will come a point when the strategy stops working. We can refuse to get older but, guess what?, we’re all getting older and the world keeps spinning. Trump, for example, will be forced to exit by the terms of the Constitution soon enough, whereas Madonna’s (possible?) departure will likely be one of choice. Peter Pan could refuse to grow up because Neverland let him but, alas, Madonna and Trump live in a less forgiving place. Even the most stubborn public figure runs into forces that cannot be stared down by sheer refusal. But that is also what makes their instinct so powerful: they understand that there is often a long stretch between the moment other people decide you are finished and the moment you actually become so. And during that stretch, one of the most effective things a person can do is refuse to rehearse his or her own obsolescence. Madonna has spent more than 40 years doing exactly that. Maybe the real trick is not staying young. Maybe it is refusing to become the past before the present has actually finished with you.
news.summary: Madonna and Trump share one rule of power: your era is harder to end when you refuse to participate in your own succession.
news.author: Anna Rahmanan

news.title: What Did Racial Gerrymandering Really Accomplish?
news.text:
There are 535 members of Congress. Representatives chosen by qualified Americans fill those seats, in a system defined by political equality and economic liberty.

The U.S. Supreme Court inverted this principle in 1986 with the Thornburg v. Gingles decision. Attempting to equalize economic outcomes, political power was unequally allocated to congressional districts drawn with a majority of black voters. This scheme aimed to right the effects of historic wrongs and drew broad support from citizens across the country.

Embedded in the decision was the racist idea that all blacks think the same, an affront to American principles. In this pre-DEI, misguided mindset, Nature’s God in our Declaration of Independence allocates sovereignty by skin color. There is no colorblind individuality our government must humble itself before, just tribes of belief.

SCOTUS reversed that disgraceful policy in April with Louisiana v. Callais, ending an era in which states were humiliatingly scrutinized — Southern states, that is — on their conformity to court-ordered racial quotas in congressional mapping. The fact that every such “majority-minority” congressional seat went to a Democrat in a Republican state, with an ever-expanding number of such districts, was presumed to be justice at work.

Democrat civil rights and congressional leaders such as Kamala Harris, Chuck Schumer, Hakeem Jeffries, and Al Sharpton have decried the Callais ruling as a return to “Jim Crow” and an attack on voting rights. Broadly speaking, they infer it is a political effort to achieve white nationalism.

A new report from RealAmerica.Vote challenges this claim. Researchers investigated outcomes for six majority-minority districts formed or protected by the early 1990s under the Voting Rights Act Section 2. Given the immense opportunity for political, educational, and economic transformation generously apportioned by the American people, what transpired? Did the opportunity for black racial blocs to choose congressional representation equalize socioeconomic conditions in those districts as compared to surrounding districts?

Six districts (AL-7, GA-5, LA-2, MS-2, SC-6, VA-3) were selected for study since they persisted throughout the duration (2000-2024) without being overturned or invalidated by the court and maintained a majority or at least a plurality of black voters throughout.

A set of “Basic” (e.g., employment) and aspirational “American Dream” needs (e.g., own a home) were used to measure the socioeconomic performance of these districts. Data were sourced from the Census for 2000 and the American Community Survey.

The districts have seen, at best, only a slight improvement in meeting basic and aspirational needs of majority-minority black districts. Recent boundary changes in GA-5 and LA-2 appear to be driving a lot of the observed improvement, so it is hard to say whether single-member minority congressional representation improved the situation at all.

Analysis resulted in examples like this chart, where the prevalence of single motherhood ranged from 39-46 percent worse in majority-minority districts than surrounding districts, for 24 years. Blacks who were stuck stayed stuck.

The data show that Democrats locked in control of densely black-populated swaths of the South for decades, failed the incredible leadership opportunity to uplift them, and used national taxpayer dollars to incentivize broken homes and government dependence over rebuilding stable families and developing economic and individual civic potential. All six majority-minority black districts studied significantly lag their peer state districts across all need areas.

With the return of colorblind political representation, we have a new opportunity. Using the great principles of our founding, including limited government, political equality, rule of law, free markets, education in American civics to build engaged citizens, and incentives to hard work such as low taxes and respect for property rights, we can engage the potential of every American who develops their God-given gifts within the framework of our social contract.

Will Callais be the Economic Emancipation Proclamation for America’s marginalized black populations? The answer depends on each of us voting for representatives who boldly support and defend our core national values of political equality and economic liberty, known to Americans as the right to pursue happiness.

news.title: GOP strategist dumps cold water on 'myth' of party fleeing Trump
news.text:
A handful of Republican candidates have caused a stir with their efforts to distance themselves from President Donald Trump, but one GOP strategist dumped cold water on the idea during an MS NOW appearance, warning that most of the party remains too "afraid" to ditch him for the time being.

With the midterms fast approaching and Trump's approval ratings hitting historic lows, some Republicans, especially those in competitive battleground districts, have begun to distance themselves from the president to varying degrees. Some, like Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds, have scrubbed mentions of Trump from their campaign sites. Others, like Florida Rep. María Elvira Salazar and Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers, have more explicitly broken with Trump's more unpopular policies.

Some, however, are warning observers not to put too much stock in this phenomenon as a growing trend. During a Monday appearance on MS NOW, Susan Del Percio, a political analyst who previously worked as a strategist for Republican lawmakers, explained why Trump is likely to hold sway over the GOP at least until he leaves office.

"We have seen Republicans from time to time step up and try and face Donald Trump head-on," Del Percio explained. "And we've seen a couple of candidates do it. But at the end of the day, most Republicans are afraid to do it because we're going to see the majority of Republican incumbents, even though it may be fewer than there are now, get reelected. And guess what? They worry about primaries in 18 months. They are afraid of Donald Trump. And the Republicans also need Donald Trump voters who are in tough districts." 

She added: "And we see that, interestingly: I look at [New York Rep.] Mike Lawler's district in Westchester that [Kamala] Harris won narrowly. But Mike Lawler is running a competitive race, and he's not afraid to embrace Trump when it works for him. And he doesn't look like he's running away from him. At the same time, he stands up to Trump when it's necessary."

Del Percio agreed with host Jonathan Lemire's response, arguing that Trump poses a risk for Republicans with his cratering approval and the fact that he has left them with "very, very, very little to run on" in the midterms, but still stressed that the party's fear of Trump is winning out.

"Until he's out of office in January of 2029, he will influence primaries; there's no question about it," she concluded. "And anyone running for president on the Republican side or U.S. Senate or Congress will be worried about [his endorsements]."

news.title: James Talarico Gets Boost From Trump Voters in New Poll
news.text: Democratic Texas Senate hopeful James Talarico has the support of a significantly higher proportion of 2024 Donald Trump voters than his Republican opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton, does from 2024 Kamala Harris voters, according to a new Big Data Poll. Democrats are hoping to flip the Senate and the House at the November midterms, either one of which would significantly impede President Trump’s ability to get legislation passed during the final two years of his second term. Winning a Senate seat from Texas, a traditional Republican stronghold, would be a major coup for the Democrats who last won a Senate race in The Lone Star State in 1988. Newsweek contacted the Talarico and Paxton Senate campaigns for comment on Monday via email outside of regular office hours. Big Data Poll Polling company Big Data Poll surveyed 698 likely Texas voters between September 24 and September 26. The headline figure is Talarico, currently a Texas State Representative, leads Paxton by 44.6 percent of the vote to 41.6 percent once voters who only “lean” toward one candidate are excluded. Notably Talarico has the support of 15 percent of voters who say they backed Trump at the 2024 presidential election, while Paxton only has the backing of 4.3 percent of those who say they voted for Harris. Similarly, 89.3 percent of 2024 Harris voters said they would support Talarico, compared to only 72.2 percent of 2024 Trump voters for Paxton. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus four percentage points. In 2024, Trump won Texas by a margin of 13.7 percentage points, with 56.2 percent of the vote against 42.5 percent for Harris. SoCal Strategies Survey The Big Data Poll findings on Talarico and Paxton’s support from 2024 presidential election campaign voters is matched by the results of a SoCal Strategies poll of 649 likely Texas voters, conducted from 12 to 13 September. This survey found Talarico has the support of 95 percent of voters who backed Harris in 2024 along with 14 percent of Trump voters from that year. By contrast, Paxton has the backing of 84 percent of 2024 Trump voters and only four percent of 2024 Harris voters. Noticeably, SoCal Strategies found Paxton performs significantly worse with 2024 Harris voters than Texas Governor Greg Abbott, who is being challenged by Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Abbott has the backing of 89 percent of 2024 Trump voters and 13 percent of Harris voters, while Hinojosa is backed by 87 percent of Harris voters and nine percent of Trump voters. Overall, the SoCal Strategies poll gave Talarico a five-point lead with 50 percent of the vote to 45 percent for Paxton. By contrast, it found Abbott lead Hinojosa by 52 percent against 44 percent. Other Polling Friday saw the publication of a Texas Public Opinion Research survey, which found Talarico was leading Paxton by five points, with 49 percent of the vote against 44 percent. This survey of 1,007 likely Texas voters was conducted between September 19 and 22 and had a 3.6 percent margin of error. However, a Texas Southern University poll of 1,200 likely Texan voters gave Talarico a lead of just two percentage point, with 47 percent of the vote to Paxton’s 45 percent. This survey was conducted between July 27 and 30. According to prediction markets Polymarket and Kalshi, Talarico’s odds of winning in November have improved dramatically over the past couple of months. Polymarket now gives Talarico a 61 percent chance of victory versus 40 percent for Paxton. By contrast, on July 28, Paxton led by 56 percent to 44 percent. Due to rounding, the percentages don’t always add up to 100. Similarly, Talarico has a 59 percent chance of getting elected on Kalshi against 41 percent for Paxton. But on July 28, Paxton was the frontrunner with a 57 percent chance of victory to Talarico’s 43 percent. Candidate Controversies Trump-endorsed Paxton has been a controversial candidate even with Texas Republicans, which could help explain why he polls notably below Governor Abbott. Paxton defeated incumbent Republican Senator John Cornyn, who branded him a “known con man and fraud” in a bitterly fought May primary runoff. Cornyn has said he will not campaign for Paxton in the Senate election. In 2023, Paxton was impeached by the GOP controlled Texas House following allegations of abuse of public trust and unfitness for office. He denied any wrongdoing and was found not guilty by the state Senate. Talarico has also attracted controversy for various comments he has made regarding Christianity. During a 2021 Texas House speech, he said “God is nonbinary,” adding: “God is both Masculine and feminine, and everything in between.” Appearing on the Active Theology podcast that same year, Talarico said: “I always think of myself as a Christian who hates Christianity, right. And, like, I always get drawn back into it because nowhere else, in no other political philosophy, in no other economic theory, do I find anything as truly radical or revolutionary as the teachings of that barefoot rabbi.” Paxton’s campaign shared a video of an AI-generated Talarico calling himself “a Christian who hates Christianity” earlier this month, but without his follow up remarks. Last week, Talarico challenged Paxton to a televised debate on Fox News during the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin. In July, Nick Maddux, Paxton’s senior campaign advisor, said “of course we are going to debate James Talarico,” but no debate has yet been scheduled. news.title: White House reinstates access to CNN, Others following judge’s order
news.text:
The White House said on Thursday it has reinstated journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico after a federal judge deemed US President Donald Trump’s ban of the three news outlets likely unconstitutional and ordered their access immediately restored.

The midday reinstatement came after a chaotic few hours earlier on Thursday when the journalists continued to be blocked from entering the White House grounds. That prompted ‌the three news organisations to request an immediate hearing before US District Judge Tim Kelly, who issued his decision overnight.

Kelly, acting in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Monday, ordered a halt to Trump’s ban for 14 days in a press freedom case that has played out over the past week in the courtroom and White House grounds.

Kelly found that the revocation of the White House credentials of the journalists “likely violated their constitutional due process rights.”

The judge, who Trump appointed in 2017 during his first presidential term, also raised doubts about the US Justice ​Department’s national security arguments for justifying the ban, noting that Trump himself had said the action was due to what the president alleged was false or negative coverage.

Hours after Kelly issued his order, CNN, MS NOW and ​Politico told the judge they remained barred, and asked for the emergency hearing. Politico said its reporter’s credentials were confiscated. An MS NOW reporter said she was blocked from the White House. CNN ⁠said some of its staff members were denied entry onto the grounds.

In response, Micah Stopperich, the director of press operations at the White House, said in a court filing that the White House began the process of reinstating press badges for ​affected reporters at 7:25 a.m., and that the “White House press team dropped badges at the entry gate for members of the press to pick up around 9:55 a.m.”

After receiving Stopperich’s declaration, the judge denied the request by the news organisations for an ​emergency hearing but gave them an opportunity to inform him of any factual developments later in the day.

The sharpest conflict yet between Trump and the press played out during a key diplomatic moment for the US president: his appearance at the United Nations General Assembly in New York and his hosting of Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

A source familiar with the White House television press pool said its members would not reinstate their coverage until the White House formally reinstates CNN to the pool. Earlier this week, they had suspended pooled coverage in solidarity with ​CNN.

There were no TV pool cameras set up for Xi’s arrival on the White House’s South Lawn on Thursday morning, and FOX News, MS NOW and CNN did not air the two leaders’ arrival ceremony live.

During Trump’s welcome of Xi to ​the White House, the president made a joke to photographers in the Oval Office about the Chinese having the friendliest press corps.

CNN is one of the five news organisations – along with ABC, CBS, FOX News and NBC – that make up the primary White House television pool. ‌They share the ⁠costs of covering the president, take turns organising coverage and provide footage to other outlets.

NATIONAL SECURITY CONCERNS

Trump announced the ban on Friday on his social media platform, saying those news organisations “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” Trump framed their reporting as a threat to US national security.

The three outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration, saying the ban violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. A coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organisations, including Reuters, later filed a legal brief supporting the three news outlets.

Kelly ordered the Trump administration ⁠to immediately return the outlets’ press passes and stop enforcing the ban for two weeks. The judge rejected the administration’s stated national security concerns.

“The record lacks factual support for defendants’ contention that the revocation of plaintiffs’ hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds,” Kelly ​wrote.

Politics (Right)

In a filing on Tuesday, the Justice Department accused the outlets of threatening national security with their coverage, citing stories about US missile stockpiles, construction of Trump’s White House ​ballroom and turnout at the recent ⁠Republican midterm convention.

Theodore Boutrous, an attorney for the three outlets, welcomed the judge’s decision in a statement, saying: “This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law.
We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”

TENSIONS WITH THE PRESS

Although other presidential administrations have battled with the press, Trump’s campaign against the media has been unprecedented. Upending decades of tradition, his White House had denied basic access to many major news organisations, launched personal attacks on journalists and filed multiple lawsuits against news organisations.

On Wednesday, an Iowa judge dismissed Trump’s 2024 lawsuit against the Des Moines Register newspaper and pollster J. Ann Selzer. Trump ​sued the Register, its parent company Gannett and Selzer over a poll published ahead of the November 2024 US election that showed Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris leading him in Iowa. Trump accused the newspaper and its longtime pollster of fraudulently misleading readers.

In his ruling Wednesday, Iowa District Judge Scott Beattie said ​the poll was legally protected speech.

news.title: SNL Season Premiere Spoofs Mamdani-Trump Friendship in Cold Open | WATCH
news.text: "Saturday Night Live" returned for its 52nd season with NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson as host, and the cold open wasted no time diving into one of the more unexpected storylines in New York politics: the surprisingly friendly dynamic between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and President Donald Trump. James Austin Johnson, the show's go-to Trump impressionist, was back in character once again. Comedian Ramy Youssef reprised his role as Mamdani, this time worried about an approaching nor'easter set to hit New York City. In the sketch, Youssef's Mamdani records a TikTok video and wonders aloud who would be reckless enough to visit him in such rough weather, only for Johnson's Trump to show up moments later. Queens Ties and a Pointed JokeThe two characters bond briefly over growing up in Queens, with Youssef's Mamdani joking he could have lived in one of Trump's old apartment buildings. Johnson's Trump shoots back a quip about Mamdani's last name, poking fun at the odd-couple friendship the sketch is built around. The scene brings in a second surprise visitor: Ashley Padilla playing Natalie Harp, described as Trump's especially loyal executive assistant, who says she rushed over from Washington, D.C. to see him. Weekend Update Takes Aim at Xi's Visit and an AI WarningLater in the episode, "Weekend Update" anchors Michael Che and Colin Jost worked through the week's political headlines, including Chinese President Xi Jinping's trip to the United States, former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigning ahead of the midterms, and the ongoing U.N. General Assembly gathering in New York. The segment also featured cast regulars Jeremy Culhane and Jane Wickline. Wickline took on the role of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has publicly pushed for slowing down AI development, portraying him as a Gollum-style figure muttering to himself about keeping control over his own invention. In the bit, Wickline's Amodei asks Che whether he'd press a hypothetical button that kills everyone if pushed. Che immediately says no, prompting a mock look of surprise from Wickline.
news.summary: "Saturday Night Live" kicked off Season 52 with Jalen Brunson hosting, opening with a cold open spoofing the surprising rapport between Trump and Mayor Mamdani.

news.title: Trump appears Sunday at the Presidents Cup golf tournament in suburban Medinah
news.text:
President Donald Trump addressed the crowd at Sunday’s Presidents Cup golf tournament in suburban Medinah, saying “Our country is doing great, better than ever before.”

Hundreds gathered at the first hole of the tournament, where Trump lauded the country’s position under his leadership and said he was looking forward to watching golf pros.

The crowd chanted “USA, USA, USA” before he took the stage, and spectators shook red, white and blue pom poms and American flags.

Trump greeted and shook hands with each pair of U.S. and international team members before they started the fifth and final round of the tournament, which started Thursday at the Medinah Country Club.

Trump was serving as the tournament’s honorary chairman, which he also did in 2017 at Liberty National Golf Club in New Jersey during his first presidency.

It’s the first time Trump has visited Illinois in his second presidency. Last time he was in the state was his inflammatory visit to the National Association of Black Journalists conference in Chicago in 2024, where he responded combatively to the moderator’s questions and ridiculed his opponent, then-Vice President Kamala Harris, for being biracial.

“I didn’t know she was Black until a number of years ago when she happened to turn Black, and now she wants to be known as Black. So I don’t know, is she Indian or is she Black?” Trump said at the time.

Harris is Black and Indian, born in Oakland, California to an Indian mother and Jamaican father.

A handful of demonstrators, both pro- and anti-Trump, gathered around 9:30 a.m. Sunday outside the tournament before Trump arrived.

news.title: Trump has blunt response to Obama’s claims a world run by women would be better
news.text:
President Donald Trump has called Barack Obama's comments about women leaders 'ridiculous' during a rant towards the press.

It's no secret that Trump and Obama aren't the best of friends, and that their views on a number of issues differ greatly. 

Earlier this week, former POTUS Obama said: “If you put women in charge of every government for like two years and then just kind of saw alright how are things going, I have a strong belief that things would — they wouldn’t be perfect — but they’d be better."

Responding to Obama's statement when asked by reporters, Trump claimed he 'loved women' although said Obama's comments were 'ridiculous.'

“I love women. I think they're great. But what a ridiculous statement that is," he responded on Saturday.

The United States has had a sitting president ever since George Washington took office on April 30, 1789. However, in those 237 years, the country has never had a female president.

Hilary Clinton came the closest in 2016, winning the popular vote against Donald Trump.

However, she lost the Electoral College to Trump 304-227.

It was reported that overall, Clinton received 65.8 million votes, compared to Trump's 62.9 million.

In 2024, Kamala Harris was the Democratic candidate against Trump, after Joe Biden withdrew from the race in July that year.

Trump won the election with 312 Electoral College votes, and was later sworn in as president for his second term. He became only the second president in US history elected to two non-consecutive terms as president.

Donald Trump told a female reporter to 'be quiet'

Despite expressing his love for women, President Trump was heard telling a female reporter to 'be quiet' on the same day.

It came after reporters surrounded the president as he left a college football game in Tennessee over the weekend.

The topic of the president banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House came up, as one reporter asked Trump whether he only wanted outlets that 'support him' in the presidential press pool.

ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox subsequently suspended presidential pool coverage.

On Thursday, a federal judge blocked Trump's decision to ban the three outlets from the Oval Office. However, this didn't stop him from banning Air Force One joining the press pack on Air Force One this weekend.

“I want real news, not fake news like you. Listen, I want real news. I love an open free press. What I don’t like is the fake press," he said.

“Do you not want tough questions?” he asked.

The president later raised his finger and told the reporter: “Wait wait, quiet," before he once again repeated that he 'doesn't like fake news.
news.summary: The president was heard telling a female reporter to 'be quiet'
